title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
💻 9.4 Continuous Linear Setting
Moving beyond binary variables, we now consider the case where instruments and treatments can take continuous values. This setting is common in economics and health research and introduces additional nuances in estimation and interpretation.

The Continuous Linear Model
Consider the following system of equations:
First Stage (Treatment equation): \[
A = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 Z + \gamma_1 U + \epsilon_A
\] Second Stage (Outcome equation): \[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A + \gamma_2 U + \epsilon_Y
\]
Where:

\(Z\): Continuous instrumental variable
\(A\): Continuous treatment variable
\(Y\): Continuous outcome
\(U\): Unobserved confounder



IV Identification in Continuous Setting
The IV estimator in the continuous case is: \[
\hat{\beta}_1^{IV} = \frac{\text{Cov}(Y,Z)}{\text{Cov}(A,Z)}
\]
This formula generalizes our binary Wald estimator. Under the three IV assumptions, this consistently estimates the causal effect \(\beta_1\).


Extended Numerical Example

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: Distance to College and Years of Education
text:
Distance to College and Years of Education
We’ll study how years of education affect log earnings, using distance to the nearest college as an instrument.
Setting:

\(Z\): Distance to nearest college (0-100 miles)
\(A\): Years of education (8-20 years)
\(Y\): Log of annual earnings

Reasoning:

Relevance: Distance affects education costs and accessibility
Exclusion: Distance shouldn’t directly affect your earnings ability
Exchangeability: Residential location (conditional on observables) is plausibly exogenous to ability

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Simulation Details

Distance reduces education by 0.03 years per mile (first stage effect)
Each year of education increases log earnings by 0.06 (6% return)
Ability affects both education and earnings, creating confounding
We add realistic random variation to make the example more realistic

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
🧭 9.5 Nonparametric Identification of Local ATE
This section introduces the most sophisticated conceptual framework for understanding what instrumental variables actually identify. We’ll develop new notation, explore principal stratification, and formally define the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE).

New Potential Notation with Instruments
To understand IV identification rigorously, we need to expand our potential outcomes framework to include potential treatments under different instrument values.
Standard Potential Outcomes: \(Y^a\) represents the potential outcome under treatment level \(a\).
IV Potential Outcomes: We also need \(A^z\) to represent the potential treatment under instrument value \(z\).

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Expanded Notation System
For each individual \(i\), we have:

\(Y_i^{A_i^0}\): Outcome they would have under their natural treatment when \(Z=0\)
\(Y_i^{A_i^1}\): Outcome they would have under their natural treatment when \(Z=1\)

\(Y_i^0\): Outcome under no treatment (traditional notation)
\(Y_i^1\): Outcome under treatment (traditional notation)
\(A_i^0\): Treatment they would choose when \(Z=0\)
\(A_i^1\): Treatment they would choose when \(Z=1\)

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
The Four Principal Strata

Compliers: \(A_i^1 = 1, A_i^0 = 0\)

Take treatment when instrument is “on”, don’t take it when instrument is “off”
These are the people influenced by the instrument

Always-takers: \(A_i^1 = 1, A_i^0 = 1\)

Take treatment regardless of instrument value
The instrument doesn’t affect their behavior

Never-takers: \(A_i^1 = 0, A_i^0 = 0\)

Never take treatment regardless of instrument value
The instrument doesn’t affect their behavior

Defiers: \(A_i^1 = 0, A_i^0 = 1\)

Do the opposite of what the instrument suggests
Usually assumed not to exist (monotonicity assumption)

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Monotonicity (No Defiers)
We assume \(A_i^1 \geq A_i^0\) for all individuals \(i\).
This means the instrument weakly increases treatment probability for everyone. No one does the opposite of what the instrument suggests.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: LATE Calculation: College and Earnings Revisited
text:
LATE Calculation: College and Earnings Revisited
Let’s work through a detailed example where we can observe the principal strata.
Population Composition: - 50% Compliers: College attendance depends on distance - 30% Always-takers: Attend college regardless of distance
- 20% Never-takers: Never attend college regardless of distance
Treatment Effects by Strata: - Compliers: \(+\$35,000\) from college - Always-takers: \(+\$25,000\) from college - Never-takers: \(+\$45,000\) from college (hypothetical - we don’t observe this)
Population ATE: \(0.5 \times 35 + 0.3 \times 25 + 0.2 \times 45 = \$34,500\)
LATE: \(\$35,000\) (effect for compliers only)

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Simulation Logic

We create the principal strata first, then generate treatment based on strata and instrument
Compliers attend college when close (Z=1), not when far (Z=0)
Always-takers attend regardless of distance
Never-takers never attend regardless of distance
Treatment effects differ across strata to show heterogeneity

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: 📌 9.6 More General Settings for ATE Identification
text:
📌 9.6 More General Settings for ATE Identification
Having established the LATE framework, we now explore when and how IV methods can identify the population Average Treatment Effect (ATE) under stronger assumptions, and examine extensions to more complex settings.

Conditions for ATE Identification
While IV generally identifies LATE, the population ATE can be recovered under special circumstances:

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
When IV Identifies ATE

Homogeneous Treatment Effects: \(Y_i^1 - Y_i^0 = \tau\) for all \(i\)

Everyone has the same treatment effect
LATE = ATE = \(\tau\)

Perfect Compliance: Everyone is a complier

\(A_i^1 = 1\) and \(A_i^0 = 0\) for all \(i\)
No always-takers or never-takers

Representative Compliers:

\(E[Y_i^1 - Y_i^0 | \text{Complier}] = E[Y_i^1 - Y_i^0]\)
Compliers have the same average treatment effect as the population

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: Multiple Instruments Example: Returns to Education
text:
Multiple Instruments Example: Returns to Education
Consider using both distance to college and tuition costs as instruments for education:

Both should satisfy exclusion restriction
Both should be correlated with education (relevance)
They may affect different complier populations

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Multiple Instruments Benefits

Using both instruments typically reduces standard errors
Provides a robustness check - estimates should be similar if assumptions hold
Allows for overidentification testing

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
❓ Check Your Understanding

Question 1
Explain why having multiple instruments allows for overidentification testing. What does it mean if this test rejects?

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Answer
With multiple instruments, we have more moment conditions than parameters to estimate - this creates “overidentification.” If all instruments are valid, they should identify the same causal parameter. The overidentification test checks whether different instruments give statistically similar estimates.
If the test rejects, it suggests that:

At least one instrument violates the exclusion restriction
The instruments identify different Local Average Treatment Effects (heterogeneous effects)
There are other specification problems

Rejection doesn’t tell us which instrument is problematic, but indicates the IV assumptions may be violated.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Answer
LATE is “local” in three ways:

Population: Only applies to compliers (those affected by the instrument)
Instrument-specific: Different instruments identify different complier populations
Context-dependent: The complier population may not be representative of policy targets

This matters for policy because:

A policy intervention might affect a different population than the instrument’s compliers
The treatment effect for policy-relevant populations might differ from LATE
External validity requires careful consideration of who the compliers are and whether they’re representative of the target population

For example, using distance to college as an instrument identifies effects for people on the margin due to access costs, but a tuition subsidy policy might affect a broader population.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Answer
IV can identify the population ATE under these conditions:

Homogeneous treatment effects: \(Y_i^1 - Y_i^0 = \tau\) for all \(i\)

Everyone has the same treatment effect
LATE = ATE = \(\tau\)

Perfect compliance: Everyone is a complier

\(A_i^1 = 1\) and \(A_i^0 = 0\) for all \(i\)
No always-takers or never-takers

Representative compliers:

\(E[Y_i^1 - Y_i^0 | \text{Complier}] = E[Y_i^1 - Y_i^0]\)
Compliers have the same average treatment effect as the population


In practice, these conditions are often strong assumptions. Condition 1 rules out interesting heterogeneity, condition 2 is rare (most instruments only affect some people), and condition 3 is hard to verify. This is why most IV applications should interpret results as LATE rather than ATE unless there’s strong justification for one of these assumptions.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Answer
OLS with unobserved confounding:

Compares people who chose different treatments
Confounded by unmeasured factors that affect both treatment choice and outcomes
Answers: “What’s the difference in outcomes between those who chose treatment vs. those who didn’t?”
Problem: This includes selection bias, not just the causal effect

IV with valid instrument:

Compares people who were encouraged vs. discouraged from treatment by a quasi-random factor
Isolates the causal effect by using exogenous variation
Answers: “What’s the effect of treatment for people whose treatment decision was influenced by this quasi-random encouragement?”
Advantage: Provides causal identification
Limitation: Only applies to the “complier” population affected by the instrument

For policy: IV gives you the causal effect, but for a specific subgroup. You need to consider whether this subgroup is relevant for your policy intervention.

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Research Question: What is the effect of a job training program (\(A\)) on income (\(Y\)), and how much of this effect is mediated through skill level (\(M\))?

Treatment (\(A\)): Job training program (\(A = 0\): no training, \(A = 1\): training)
Mediator (\(M\)): Skill level (continuous scale 0–100)
Outcome (\(Y\)): Annual income (in thousands)
Sample size: \(n = 1{,}000\) individuals

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Research Question: What is the effect of a job training program (\(A\)) on income (\(Y\)), and how much of this effect is mediated through skill level (\(M\))?

Treatment (\(A\)): Job training program (\(A = 0\): no training, \(A = 1\): training)
Mediator (\(M\)): Skill level (continuous scale 0–100)
Outcome (\(Y\)): Annual income (in thousands)
Sample size: \(n = 1{,}000\) individuals

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Generating Models
The following are generating models for observed outcomes, which under consistency also determine the potential outcomes \(M^{a}\) and \(Y^{a, m}\).

Mediator Model (for \(M\), a Function of \(A\))
\[
M = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 A + \varepsilon_M
\]

\(\alpha_0 = 60\): baseline skill level
\(\alpha_1 = 15\): effect of training on skills

From this model:

\(M^1 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 = 75\)
\(M^0 = \alpha_0 = 60\)



Outcome Model (for \(Y\), as a Function of \(A\), \(M\), and \(A \cdot M\))
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A + \beta_2 M + \beta_3 A M + \varepsilon_Y
\]

\(\beta_0 = 30\): baseline income
\(\beta_1 = 8\): direct effect of training
\(\beta_2 = 0.4\): effect of skills on income
\(\beta_3 = 0.1\): interaction effect between training and skills

text:

CAUSAL EFFECTS

\(Y^{1, M^0} - Y^{0, M^0}\)

\(Y^{1, M^1} - Y^{1, M^0}\)

\(Y^{1, M^1} - Y^{0, M^0}\)
\(75.5 - 54.0\)

Alternative NIE

NDE + NIE = TE?

PROPORTIONS





% Mediated

\(\frac{7.5}{21.5} \times 100\)

\(\frac{14.0}{21.5} \times 100\)

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Interpretation

Key Findings

Total Effect: The job training program increases income by $21,500 on average.
Natural Direct Effect: $14,000 (65.1%) of the effect operates through pathways other than skill improvement.
Natural Indirect Effect: $7,500 (34.9%) of the effect is mediated via increased skill levels.
Mediation: Roughly one-third of the program’s benefit comes from skill enhancement.



Counterfactual Interpretation

\(Y^{1, M^1} = 75.5\): Income if treated and skill develops as it would under treatment.
\(Y^{1, M^0} = 68.0\): Income if treated but with skill level that would occur under no treatment.
\(Y^{0, M^1} = 60.0\): Income if untreated but skill level is as if treated.
\(Y^{0, M^0} = 54.0\): Income if untreated and skill level is as under no treatment.



Policy Implications

The program has direct effects beyond skills (e.g., networking, confidence, signaling).
The mediator (skills) contributes significantly but is not the dominant pathway.
Interventions should support both skill acquisition and broader contextual benefits.

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Technical Notes

These are structural models for observed variables that also imply counterfactuals under consistency and ignorability.
The interaction term \(\beta_3 = 0.1\) introduces non-additivity across treatment levels.
The alternative NIE (e.g., \(Y^{0, M^1} - Y^{0, M^0}\)) differs due to this interaction.
Inference procedures (e.g., bootstrapping or delta method) and sensitivity analyses are required in practice.

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Model Setup
We assume the following structural equations:

Mediator Model
\[
M = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 A + \varepsilon_M
\]

\(\alpha_0 = 60\), \(\alpha_1 = 15\)



Outcome Model
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A + \beta_2 M + \beta_3 A \cdot M + \varepsilon_Y
\]

\(\beta_0 = 30\), \(\beta_1 = 8\), \(\beta_2 = 0.4\), \(\beta_3 = 0.1\)

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Interpretation

The Total Effect for individual 1 is 21.5, which is decomposed into:

Natural Direct Effect: 14.0 (not mediated by skill)
Natural Indirect Effect: 7.5 (mediated through skill development)

The proportion mediated is:

\[
\frac{\text{NIE}}{\text{TE}} = \frac{7.5}{21.5} \approx 34.9\%
\]

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Observations Across Individuals

All individuals show similar NIE due to the same change in mediator under treatment (\(\Delta M = 15\)).
Variation in TE is driven by individual residuals \(\varepsilon_M\) and \(\varepsilon_Y\).
Slight differences in NDE and TE arise from heterogeneity introduced through \(\varepsilon_Y\) and the interaction term \(\beta_3 A M\).

title: Mediation Analysis Example
text:
Summary
This example illustrates how to use structural models to simulate potential outcomes and decompose the total causal effect into direct and indirect components for each unit. These unit-level calculations help reveal individual heterogeneity in response to interventions—crucial in personalized medicine, education, or employment policy evaluation.

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text: Framed as a Target Trial Emulation

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Purpose
The final project is designed to integrate conceptual, methodological, and applied skills in causal inference. Students will pose and answer a causal question using real or simulated data, grounding their analysis in the target trial emulation framework.
The project should demonstrate:

Clear articulation of a STAT 579 Final Project Guidelinesusal estimand (not just a statistical parameter).
Careful identification strategy with explicit assumptions.
Implementation of at least one modern estimation method (e.g., IPW, matching, IV, MSM).
Critical sensitivity checks and interpretation within a real-world context.

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Timeline & Deliverables

Week 1–2: Causal Question Definition

Submit a 1–2 paragraph causal question relevant to biostatistics, epidemiology, or social/biomedical sciences.
Include justification of why the question is causal (not associational).

Week 3–4: Preliminary DAG

Provide a directed acyclic graph (using dagitty or ggdag).
State which paths must be blocked for identification.
Identify potential sources of bias (confounding, selection, measurement error).

Week 5–6: Identification Strategy

Explicitly state whether exchangeability, positivity, SUTVA, and consistency are plausible.
Describe your strategy: backdoor adjustment, IV, MSM, or mediation.

Week 9: Project Proposal (10% of course grade)

3–5 pages.
Elements:

Research question & target trial specification (eligibility, treatment strategies, follow-up, outcome).
DAG & assumptions.
Identification strategy.
Planned data source (public dataset, your own research, or simulation).
Anticipated challenges.


Weeks 10–13: Analysis

Implement at least one causal method (e.g., IPW, g-computation, IV, mediation, MSM).
Provide R code and output with clear interpretation.
Conduct diagnostics (balance checks, overlap, weak instrument tests, model fit).
Perform at least one sensitivity analysis (e.g., E-values, Rosenbaum bounds, tipr).

Week 14: Presentation (10%)

12–15 minutes, conference-style.
Emphasize assumptions, robustness, and substantive conclusions—not just technical detail.

Final Paper (25%) – Due Finals Week

~12–15 pages, structured as a research article:

Introduction: Causal question and motivation.
Target Trial Protocol: Eligibility, treatment, follow-up, outcome, causal estimand.
Assumptions & Identification: DAG, assumptions, strategy.
Methods: Data source, causal methods used, software.
Results: Estimates, sensitivity analyses, robustness checks.
Discussion: Interpretation, limitations, implications.
Appendix: R code (clean, annotated).

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Detailed Instructions

Step 1: Choosing a Question

Prefer health, social, or biomedical contexts (e.g., effect of smoking on lung cancer, impact of job training on income, role of diet on heart disease).
The question must be causal, not descriptive.

Bad: “What factors are associated with depression?”
Good: “What is the effect of exercise on reducing depression severity?”




Step 2: DAG Construction

Must use dagitty or ggdag.
Include confounders, colliders, mediators, and selection mechanisms.
Explicitly identify adjustment set(s) and whether positivity holds.



Step 3: Identification & Assumptions

Address the three pillars:

Exchangeability (unconfoundedness, or IV/exclusion restriction justification).
Positivity (overlap diagnostics, trimming if needed).
Consistency & SUTVA (intervention is well-defined).




Step 4: Method Implementation

Choose a method appropriate to your design:

Backdoor adjustment: matching, stratification, regression, IPW.
IV: LATE, 2SLS.
Mediation: NDE/NIE decomposition.
MSM: time-varying exposures.

Use R packages: MatchIt, WeightIt, ivreg, mediation, EValue, tipr.



Step 5: Sensitivity Analysis

Required to evaluate robustness. Options:

E-value.
Rosenbaum bounds.
Simulated confounding (tipr).




Step 6: Writing & Presentation

Clarity of assumptions is more important than fancy methods.
Discussion must explicitly state: “If assumption X fails, my estimate is biased because…”

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Evaluation Criteria

Question & Relevance (10%): Is the question causal and well-motivated?
DAG & Identification (20%): Correct, complete, and clearly explained.
Methodology (20%): Appropriate method, correct implementation, diagnostics.
Sensitivity & Robustness (15%): At least one sensitivity analysis, well-interpreted.
Results & Interpretation (15%): Clear, correct, cautious interpretation.
Writing & Presentation (20%): Organization, clarity, reproducibility.

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
References for Guidance

Hernán & Robins (2024). Causal Inference: What If.
Neal (2020). Introduction to Causal Inference.
Imbens & Rubin (2015). Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences.
Brumback (2022). Fundamentals of Causal Inference with R.
VanderWeele (2015). Explanation in Causal Inference.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
text:
Imagine we have a large electronic health record (EHR) dataset and we want to answer the question: “Does taking statins prevent cardiovascular disease (CVD)?”


A traditional approach might look like this:

Data First: Open the dataset. Identify a variable for “statin use” (e.g., statin_ever_used) and an outcome variable for “CVD.”
Model: Choose a regression model. Let’s use logistic regression: CVD ~ statin_ever_used + age + sex + diabetes.
Result: Fit the model. Look at the odds ratio for statin_ever_used. If it’s less than 1 and the p-value is significant, conclude that statins are protective.

This seems straightforward, but it is filled with hidden pitfalls. The causal question is vague, and the analysis is susceptible to numerous biases that are difficult to see without a more structured framework.



The TTE framework forces us to change our entire workflow.

Mindset Shift: We start with the question, not the data. Our first step is to design the ideal, hypothetical randomized controlled trial (RCT) we wish we could run to answer our question. This is our “target trial.” Only after we have a complete “protocol” for this ideal trial do we turn to the observational data and see how well we can emulate it.

This disciplined process makes our assumptions explicit and helps us proactively design an analysis that avoids common biases.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
section: Tutorial: Building the Target Trial Protocol
text:
Tutorial: Building the Target Trial Protocol
The protocol of any trial (real or hypothetical) has key components. Let’s define them for our statin/CVD question and contrast the TTE approach with the “just analyze” approach at each step.

1. Eligibility Criteria

The Question: Who would be eligible to enroll in our ideal trial?
“Just Analyze” Approach: This is often an afterthought. We might just use all patients in the dataset who don’t have missing values for our variables of interest.
TTE Approach: We must be explicit. For our statin trial, we might specify:

Inclusion: Patients aged 40-75.
Exclusion: Patients with a history of CVD at baseline (since we’re studying prevention). Patients without continuous health plan enrollment for the prior year (to ensure we have their baseline data).
Why it matters: Excluding prevalent users (those already on statins) and requiring a clean baseline period is crucial for avoiding selection bias and ensuring we are comparing apples to apples.




2. Treatment Strategies

The Question: What are the precise interventions we are comparing?
“Just Analyze” Approach: We might use a vague statin_ever_used variable. But what does this mean? Did they take one pill? Take it for 10 years? This ambiguity is a major source of error.
TTE Approach: We must specify the strategies precisely, as in a real trial.

Strategy 1: Initiate a statin (e.g., atorvastatin, simvastatin) at baseline.
Strategy 2: Do not initiate a statin at baseline.
Why it matters: This pushes us towards a “new-user” design, where we only include patients at the moment they become eligible to start the therapy. This is a powerful tool to prevent biases.




3. Assignment Procedure

The Question: How are individuals assigned to a treatment strategy?
“Just Analyze” Approach: The assignment is whatever happened in the real world. We hope to “control for confounding” by adding covariates to a regression model.
TTE Approach: In our ideal target trial, we would assign treatment randomly at baseline. In the real world, this is obviously not the case; doctors assign statins for reasons (confounding). Our task is to emulate randomization. We do this by adjusting for a sufficient set of baseline confounders (identified by our DAG!) using methods like:

Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW): Creating a “pseudo-population” where the confounders are no longer associated with treatment assignment.
Matching: Matching treated individuals to untreated individuals with similar baseline characteristics.
Why it matters: This makes the goal of “controlling for confounding” a deliberate design choice, not just a modeling exercise. We are explicitly trying to create groups that are exchangeable, just like in a real RCT.




4. Follow-up Period

The Question: When does follow-up begin and end?
“Just Analyze” Approach: The start of follow-up is often poorly defined. Does it start when the patient enters the database? Or when they first use a statin?
TTE Approach: The start of follow-up (time zero) must be the same for everyone: the moment of treatment assignment (or emulation of assignment).

For new users, this is the date of their first statin prescription.
For non-users, we can assign a similar “index date.”
Follow-up ends at a pre-specified time (e.g., 5 years), or when CVD occurs, or when they leave the health plan (censoring).
Why it matters: Properly defining time zero is the single most effective way to prevent immortal time bias. This bias occurs when a period of follow-up is misclassified as “unexposed” when it should be “not yet exposed,” leading to a spurious protective effect.




5. Outcome

The Question: How do we define the outcome?
TTE Approach: We need to specify the outcome just as we would in a trial protocol (e.g., “first diagnosis of a myocardial infarction or stroke, identified via ICD-10 codes during an inpatient hospital stay”). This clarity reduces measurement error.



6. Causal Contrasts (Estimand)

The Question: What is the precise causal effect we are trying to estimate?
“Just Analyze” Approach: This is often implicit in the model output (e.g., an odds ratio).
TTE Approach: We specify our estimand up front. The two main choices are:

Intention-to-Treat (ITT) effect: The effect of assigning the treatment strategy at baseline, regardless of whether the patient adheres to it later. This is often emulated in observational data.
Per-Protocol effect: The effect of adhering to the treatment strategy over time. This is more complex and requires advanced methods like Marginal Structural Models (MSMs) to handle time-varying confounding.
Why it matters: Being explicit about the estimand dictates the correct analysis plan and prevents misinterpretation of the results.




7. Analysis Plan

The Question: How will we estimate the causal contrast?
“Just Analyze” Approach: Fit a single regression model.
TTE Approach: The analysis plan flows directly from all the previous design choices. If emulating an ITT effect, we might use a weighted Cox model (using IPTW) that compares the two groups from time zero. If estimating a per-protocol effect, we would need to specify how we will handle treatment switching and censoring.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
section: Summary: Why Target Trial Emulation is Different
text:
Summary: Why Target Trial Emulation is Different








Feature
“Just Analyzing Data”
Target Trial Emulation




Starting Point
The dataset and its variables
A precise causal question & an ideal trial protocol


Assumptions
Often implicit, hidden in the model
Explicitly stated in the protocol design


Bias Avoidance
Reactive (hope regression “controls” for it)
Proactive (design choices to prevent bias)


Transparency
Low; it’s hard to know exactly what was compared
High; the emulated protocol is the roadmap for the analysis


Rigor
Variable; prone to hidden errors
High; provides a systematic framework



In short, target trial emulation is not a statistical method. It’s a structured way of thinking. It’s the overarching framework that guides you to ask the right questions, design a sound observational analysis, choose the right statistical methods, and avoid preventable biases. It turns a simple data analysis into a credible scientific investigation.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
text:
Trial Emulation Example
Here are the seven components of a target trial designed to answer the question: “What is the effect of obtaining a bachelor’s degree on personal income?”

1. Eligibility Criteria
This defines the population for our hypothetical trial. We can’t include everyone. We need a specific cohort of people who are at the point of making the decision.

Eligible Population: All individuals who graduated from a U.S. high school in a specific year (e.g., 2010), are between 17-19 years old at graduation, and have not yet enrolled in a 4-year college program.
Exclusions: Individuals who are not eligible to apply to a 4-year college or who already possess an associate’s degree or other advanced vocational certification.



2. Treatment Strategies
These are the precise interventions we want to compare. “Getting a degree” is too vague.

Strategy 1 (Treated): Enroll in a 4-year bachelor’s degree program within one year of high school graduation and successfully obtain a bachelor’s degree within six years of high school graduation.
Strategy 2 (Control): Do not obtain a bachelor’s degree within six years of high school graduation. (This group may enter the workforce, attend community college, or pursue vocational training.)



3. Assignment Procedure
In an ideal world, we would randomize. In our emulation, we mimic that randomization.

Ideal Trial: Eligible individuals would be randomly assigned at high school graduation to either pursue the “degree” strategy or the “no degree” strategy.
Emulation: We use observational data and adjust for the baseline factors that influence both the decision to attend college and future income. This is our confounder set. We would use methods like propensity score weighting or matching to balance the two groups on key baseline variables measured at high school graduation, such as:

High School GPA and class rank
Standardized test scores (SAT/ACT)
Family income and socioeconomic status
Parental education level
High school quality and resources




4. Follow-up Period
This defines the timeline for our study, and time zero is critical.

Start of Follow-up (Time Zero): The clock starts for everyone at the same moment: right after high school graduation (e.g., September 1, 2010). This is the point of (emulated) randomization.
End of Follow-up: The follow-up period ends when the outcome is measured. A reasonable point would be 12 years after high school graduation, when individuals are approximately 30 years old and have had time to establish themselves in their careers.



5. Outcome
This is the specific event we are measuring.

Primary Outcome: Annual personal pre-tax income at age 30, measured in U.S. dollars. The data source (e.g., tax records, survey data) must be specified.



6. Causal Contrasts (Estimand)
This is the specific statistical quantity we aim to estimate.

Estimand: The Average Treatment Effect (ATE). Specifically, we want to calculate the difference in mean annual income at age 30 between the group assigned to Strategy 1 and the group assigned to Strategy 2. This is an “intention-to-treat” estimand, as it measures the effect of being assigned to a strategy at baseline, regardless of eventual adherence (e.g., some people assigned to the college track might drop out).



7. Analysis Plan
This outlines the statistical steps to estimate the causal contrast.

The Plan:

Among the eligible cohort of 2010 high school graduates, fit a model (e.g., logistic regression) to estimate each person’s probability of attending college based on the baseline confounders (GPA, family income, etc.). This yields the propensity score.
Use these propensity scores to calculate inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) to create a pseudo-population where the baseline confounders are balanced between the two groups.
In this weighted pseudo-population, calculate the mean income at age 30 in the group that obtained a degree and the group that did not.
The difference between these two means is the estimate of the causal effect. We would then calculate a 95% confidence interval around this estimate.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
text:
The goal when reading a methodological paper is not to memorize every formula but to build a robust mental model of the author’s argument. You want to understand the problem they solved, the logic of their solution, the assumptions required for it to work, and its ultimate impact. This active, model-building approach is far more effective than passive reading.
We will use a Three-Pass Approach designed to manage cognitive load and build your understanding from a scaffold to a fully-formed structure.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 1: The Bird’s-Eye View – Building the Scaffold (15 Minutes) 🗺️
text:
Pass 1: The Bird’s-Eye View – Building the Scaffold (15 Minutes) 🗺️
Don’t start by reading page one. Your first goal is to create a mental “map” of the paper’s purpose and structure. This provides a scaffold for your brain to hang the details on later, which significantly reduces cognitive load.

Read the Abstract, Introduction, and Conclusion First: Read these three sections carefully. At the end of this step, you should be able to answer, in simple terms:

The Problem: What specific challenge or gap in knowledge existed before this paper was written?
The Solution: What is the main idea, method, or framework this paper proposes?
The Claim: What do the authors claim is the primary impact or takeaway of their work?

Scan the Section Headings: Look at the structure of the paper. How do the authors build their argument from the problem to the solution?
Examine Figures and Conceptual Tables: Look at any diagrams (like DAGs), charts, or conceptual tables. Read their captions. These often contain the most important ideas in a condensed, visual format.

At the end of this pass, you shouldn’t understand the details, but you should have a clear sense of the paper’s story.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 2: The Deep Dive – Adding the Bricks with Active Recall (1-2 Hours) 🧱
text:
Pass 2: The Deep Dive – Adding the Bricks with Active Recall (1-2 Hours) 🧱
Now, read the paper from start to finish, but with an active, questioning mindset. Your goal is to deconstruct the argument, not just consume it.

“Translate” the Math: When you encounter a block of equations, your goal is not to re-derive the proofs. Instead, focus on the English sentences before and after the math. Your task is to translate the mathematical statement into a conceptual one. For example, when you see the formula for the propensity score, you should translate it in your notes as: “This is the probability of getting the treatment, given the measured covariates L.”
Focus on the Assumptions: For causal inference papers, assumptions are the most important part. They are the weak points of any argument. When an assumption is stated (e.g., “unconfoundedness,” “exclusion restriction”), stop and ask:

What does this assumption mean conceptually?
Why is it necessary for the author’s argument to work?
Is this assumption testable? If not, in what real-world scenarios might it be plausible or implausible?

Engage in Active Recall: After reading each major section, stop, look away from the page, and ask yourself: “What was the single most important point of that section?” Try to summarize it in one or two sentences, either in your head or in your notes. This act of forcing your brain to retrieve the information is far more powerful for learning than passively re-reading the text.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 3: The Feynman Technique – Solidifying Understanding (30 Minutes) ✍️
text:
Pass 3: The Feynman Technique – Solidifying Understanding (30 Minutes) ✍️
You only truly understand something when you can explain it simply. This final pass solidifies your mental model and reveals any remaining gaps in your knowledge.

Put the paper away. Open a blank document or grab a piece of paper.
Explain the paper to an imaginary first-year graduate student. Your explanation must clearly and simply answer the following five questions:

What was the central problem the authors were trying to solve?
What was their key insight or proposed solution?
In simple terms, what is the core logic for why their solution works?
What are the 1-3 critical assumptions it relies on to be valid?
What is the single biggest limitation or most important implication of this work?


If you get stuck or find yourself using jargon you can’t define, you’ve found the edge of your understanding. Go back to the paper and focus specifically on that part. This technique is the most efficient way to build deep, lasting comprehension.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Example Application: The Feynman Technique for Week 5 (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983)
text:
Example Application: The Feynman Technique for Week 5 (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983)
After reading the paper, your Feynman explanation might look like this:

Problem: In observational studies, people who get a treatment are different from those who don’t across many variables (confounders). Trying to adjust for all of them in a single regression model is complicated and non-transparent.
Solution: They proposed the propensity score—the probability of getting treated given your set of covariates. They proved you only need to adjust for this single number to remove bias from all observed confounders.
Logic: The propensity score has a “balancing property.” At any given value of the score, the distribution of the covariates is the same between the treated and untreated groups, just like in a randomized experiment.
Assumptions: This only works if you’ve measured all the important confounders (unconfoundedness) and if there are both treated and untreated people at every level of the propensity score (positivity/overlap). Unconfoundedness is a huge, untestable assumption.
Impact: This revolutionized observational research by creating a two-step process: first, focus on study design by creating balanced groups, and only then, perform the outcome analysis. Its biggest limitation is that it does nothing to solve the problem of unmeasured confounders.

title: Weekly Paper Critique Schedule
text:
Each week, you are assigned two papers: a Classic paper that established a foundational concept and a Modern paper that extends, applies, or reframes that concept. You are expected to be familiar with both for our class discussions.
For each paper, read the provided summary and prepare written responses to the three guiding questions. Bring your notes to class to support discussion and critiques.

title: Weekly Paper Critique Schedule
text:
Each week, you are assigned two papers: a Classic paper that established a foundational concept and a Modern paper that extends, applies, or reframes that concept. You are expected to be familiar with both for our class discussions.
For each paper, read the provided summary and prepare written responses to the three guiding questions. Bring your notes to class to support discussion and critiques.

title: Weekly Paper Critique Schedule
text:
Part I: Foundations

Week 1 – Causal Effects & SUTVA

Classic: Rubin, D. B. (1974). Estimating causal effects of treatments in randomized and nonrandomized studies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 66(5), 688–701. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0037350
Summary: Introduces the potential outcomes framework, defines causal effects as counterfactual contrasts, and articulates the “fundamental problem of causal inference.”
Questions:

In your own words, what is the fundamental problem of causal inference?

Why is the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) necessary? Give a real-world example of violation.

How does this framework clarify the difference between causal effects and observed associations?

Modern: Rubin, D. B. (2005). Causal inference using potential outcomes: Design, modeling, decisions. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 100(469), 322–331. https://doi.org/10.1198/016214504000001880
Summary: Reflects on the evolution of the framework, emphasizing “design trumps analysis” and transparency of assumptions.
Questions:

What does Rubin mean by “design trumps analysis”? Provide an example.

How does the framework make assumptions explicit compared to regression?

What challenges arise when prioritizing design in observational studies?




Week 2 – DAGs

Classic: Greenland, S., Pearl, J., & Robins, J. M. (1999). Causal diagrams for epidemiologic research. Epidemiology, 10(1), 37–48. https://doi.org/10.1097/00001648-199901000-00008
Summary: Introduces Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) as a language for representing causal assumptions and identifying confounding, colliders, and valid adjustment sets.
Questions:

Draw a DAG for your own research area, identifying one confounder, one mediator, and one collider.

What is the back-door criterion, and why does it justify covariate adjustment?

Why is conditioning on a collider problematic? Provide an example.

Modern: Textor, J., van der Zander, B., Gilthorpe, M. S., Liśkiewicz, M., & Ellison, G. T. H. (2016). Robust causal inference using directed acyclic graphs: The R package dagitty. International Journal of Epidemiology, 45(6), 1887–1894. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw341
Summary: Introduces dagitty, a tool to automate adjustment set selection, evaluate testable implications, and visualize DAGs.
Questions:

What are the advantages of using dagitty versus manual identification?

How do testable implications help assess a DAG?

What limitations remain in relying on software for causal modeling?




Week 3 – Exchangeability / Positivity / Consistency

Classic: Holland, P. W. (1986). Statistics and causal inference. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 81(396), 945–960. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1986.10478354
Summary: Clarifies Rubin’s model by distinguishing association vs. causation, stressing “no causation without manipulation,” and outlining assumptions of exchangeability, positivity, and consistency.
Questions:

How does “no causation without manipulation” distinguish causes from attributes?

What are the three core assumptions for causal inference?

Which assumption is hardest to verify in practice, and why?

Modern: Hernán, M. A. (2018). The C-word: Scientific euphemisms do not improve causal inference from observational data. American Journal of Public Health, 108(5), 616–619. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2018.304337
Summary: Critiques euphemisms like “associated with,” arguing that explicit causal language enforces clarity about assumptions.
Questions:

What risks arise from using causal euphemisms?

Do you agree with Hernán that researchers should always say “cause”? Why or why not?

When might it be valid to avoid causal language?




Week 4 – Confounding & Selection Bias

Classic: Hernán, M. A., Hernández-Díaz, S., & Robins, J. M. (2004). A structural approach to selection bias. Epidemiology, 15(5), 615–625. https://doi.org/10.1097/01.ede.0000135174.63482.43
Summary: Provides a unified framework for selection bias using DAGs, showing how many biases (Berkson’s bias, loss-to-follow-up) arise from conditioning on a collider.
Questions:

Draw a DAG illustrating how restricting to hospitalized patients induces spurious associations.

How can loss-to-follow-up be represented in a DAG, and under what conditions does it bias estimates?

Why is collider bias a unifying explanation for many selection biases?

Modern: Cole, S. R., & Hernán, M. A. (2002). Fallibility in estimating direct effects. International Journal of Epidemiology, 31(1), 163–165. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/31.1.163
Summary: Demonstrates via DAGs that adjusting for mediators with regression can misestimate direct effects if there is unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding.
Questions:

Why does the standard regression approach to mediation often fail?

How does unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding complicate direct effect estimation?

How does this set the stage for modern causal mediation analysis?

title: Weekly Paper Critique Schedule
text:
Part II: Estimation Methods

Week 5 – Propensity Scores
Classic : Rosenbaum, P. R., & Rubin, D. B. (1983). The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects. Biometrika, 70(1), 41–55. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/70.1.41. Stable links: OUP; JSTOR. Oxford Academic JSTOR
Summary.
Proves that the propensity score is a balancing score, and that conditioning on it suffices to remove bias from observed covariates under strong ignorability. Lays foundations for matching, subclassification, IPTW, and covariate adjustment via the score. 24Oxford Academic
Critique questions.

Provide diagnostics to verify the balancing property in finite samples—what failures most threaten bias/variance?

Under which sampling regimes does trimming (lack of overlap) improve MSE yet alter the estimand?

Discuss the limits of propensity scores under interference or measurement error in covariates.

Modern:
Austin, P. C. (2011). An introduction to propensity score methods for reducing the effects of confounding in observational studies. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 46(3), 399–424. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2011.568786. Stable links: PubMed/PMC. 25PubMed PMC
Summary.
Reviews four implementations (matching, stratification, IPTW, regression adjustment) and stresses balance diagnostics and overlap checks. Offers pragmatic guidance for implementation choices and reporting. PMC
Critique questions.

Compare nearest-neighbor matching vs. IPTW for ATE/ATT under severe imbalance; which estimand is recovered, and at what variance cost?

What constitutes adequate common support? Propose quantitative thresholds and a pre-registered trimming rule.

Evaluate post-matching outcome modeling: when does it help vs. reintroduce model dependence?



Week 6 – IPTW & Marginal Structural Models

Classic:
Robins, J. M., Hernán, M. A., & Brumback, B. (2000). Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology, 11(5), 550–560. https://doi.org/10.1097/00001648-200009000-00011
Summary: Introduces MSMs and IPTW to adjust for time-varying confounding affected by prior treatment.
Questions:

Why does standard regression fail when confounders are also mediators?

What is the pseudo-population created by IPTW, and how does it help?

What are key limitations of MSMs in practice?

Modern: Cole, S. R., & Hernán, M. A. (2008). Constructing inverse probability weights for marginal structural models. American Journal of Epidemiology, 168(6), 656–664. https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwn164
Summary: Provides step-by-step guidance on constructing stabilized IPTWs and diagnostics.
Questions:

Why are stabilized weights preferred over unstabilized?

What diagnostic checks are necessary after weighting?

How do extreme weights undermine MSM results?




Week 7 – G-computation & TMLE

Classic: Robins, J. M. (1986). A new approach to causal inference in mortality studies with sustained exposure periods—application of the G-formula. Mathematical Modelling, 7(9–12), 1393–1512. https://doi.org/10.1016/0270-0255(86)90088-6
Summary: Introduces the g-formula for estimating causal effects of time-varying exposures using outcome modeling under interventions.
Questions:

How does g-computation differ from IPTW?

What is sequential exchangeability, and why is it critical?

What are the pros/cons of outcome-modeling approaches?

Modern: Petersen, M. L., & van der Laan, M. J. (2014). Causal models and learning from data: Integrating causal modeling and statistical estimation. Epidemiology, 25(3), 418–426. https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000000078
Summary: Describes Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (TMLE), a doubly robust method combining causal models with efficient estimation.
Questions:

What does “doubly robust” mean in practice?

How does TMLE improve on g-computation?

Why separate identification from estimation in causal analysis?




Week 8 – Instrumental Variables

Classic: Angrist, J. D. (1990). Lifetime earnings and the Vietnam era draft lottery: Evidence from social security administrative records. American Economic Review, 80(3), 313–336. http://www.jstor.org/stable/2006669
Summary: Uses the Vietnam draft lottery as an instrument to estimate the causal effect of military service on earnings.
Questions:

What three assumptions must hold for a valid instrument?

Who are the “compliers,” and why does IV identify their effect?

Which IV assumption is least plausible here?

Modern: Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J.-S. (2010). The credibility revolution in empirical economics. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 24(2), 3–30. https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.24.2.3
Summary: Argues that modern applied economics has shifted to emphasize credible research designs (IV, RD, DiD).
Questions:

What is the “credibility revolution”?

How does design alter the role of modeling in causal inference?

What risks exist in over-reliance on quasi-experiments?

title: Weekly Paper Critique Schedule
text:
Part III: Advanced Topics

Week 9 – Effect Modification & Interaction

Classic:
Rothman, K. J. (1974). Synergy and antagonism in cause–effect relationships. American Journal of Epidemiology, 99(6), 385–388. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a121617
Summary: Introduces the sufficient-component cause (“causal pies”) model, framing synergy and antagonism among causes.
Questions:

How can two factors show additive but not multiplicative interaction?

How does the causal pie model explain effect heterogeneity?

Why is additive interaction often more relevant in public health?

Modern: VanderWeele, T. J. (2019). Principles of effect modification and interaction. International Journal of Epidemiology, 48(1), 301–308. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyy276
Summary: Clarifies interaction concepts, advocating for additive-scale measures and subgroup reporting.
Questions:

Why report subgroup-specific effects instead of only an interaction p-value?

Distinguish “effect modification” from “statistical interaction.”

How does effect modification inform policy?




Week 10 – Mediation I

Classic:
Baron, R. M., & Kenny, D. A. (1986). The moderator–mediator variable distinction in social psychological research. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 51(6), 1173–1182. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.51.6.1173
Summary: Proposes the traditional four-step regression-based framework for mediation.
Questions:

What are the four Baron–Kenny steps?

What hidden assumptions are needed for causal interpretation?

Why is this approach now considered insufficient?

Modern: Imai, K., Keele, L., & Tingley, D. (2010). A general approach to causal mediation analysis. Psychological Methods, 15(4), 309–334. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0020761
Summary: Develops a potential outcomes framework for mediation, defining natural direct/indirect effects under sequential ignorability.
Questions:

What is sequential ignorability, and why is it strong?

How do natural effects improve on Baron–Kenny?

What challenges arise in applying this approach?




Week 11 – Mediation II & Principal Stratification

Classic:
Robins, J. M., & Greenland, S. (1992). Identifiability and exchangeability for direct and indirect effects. Epidemiology, 3(2), 143–155. https://doi.org/10.1097/00001648-199203000-00013
Summary: Provides counterfactual definitions of direct/indirect effects, requiring sequential exchangeability and no exposure–mediator interaction.
Questions:

What are the two parts of sequential exchangeability?

Why does exposure–mediator interaction block nonparametric identification?

How does this extend mediation beyond Baron–Kenny?

Modern: Daniel, R. M., De Stavola, B. L., Cousens, S. N., & Vansteelandt, S. (2015). Causal mediation analysis with multiple mediators. Epidemiology, 26(3), 364–372. https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000000253
Summary: Extends mediation analysis to multiple, possibly correlated mediators, introducing assumptions for path-specific effects.
Questions:

Why can’t indirect effects from separate single-mediator models be summed?

What new assumptions are needed for path-specific effects?

How does this reflect real-world complexity?




Week 12 – Sensitivity Analysis

Classic:
Rosenbaum, P. R. (1987). Sensitivity analysis for matched observational studies. Biometrika, 74(1), 13–26. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/74.1.13
Summary: Introduces sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding in matched studies, quantifying how strong a hidden confounder must be to change conclusions.
Questions:

What is the key idea behind Rosenbaum’s sensitivity analysis?

Why is sensitivity analysis critical in observational causal studies?

How might this framework be adapted for non-matched designs?

Modern: VanderWeele, T. J., & Ding, P. (2017). Sensitivity analysis in observational research: Introducing the E-value. Annals of Internal Medicine, 167(4), 268–274. https://doi.org/10.7326/M16-2607
Summary: Proposes the E-value, a simple measure of how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away an observed association.
Questions:

How do you interpret an E-value of 3.0 for a risk ratio of 2.0?

What are the assumptions behind the E-value?

What are its limitations compared to full sensitivity analyses?




Week 13 – Target Trial Emulation

Classic: Robins, J. M. (1987). A graphical approach to the identification and estimation of causal parameters in mortality studies with sustained exposure periods. Journal of Chronic Diseases, 40(Suppl. 2), 139S–161S. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0021-9681(87)80033-0
Summary: Early graphical framework showing how observational data can emulate randomized trials with sequential treatments.
Questions:

Why emulate a randomized trial with observational data?

What is this paper’s key conceptual contribution?

How do DAGs/graphs assist in this setting?

Modern: Hernán, M. A., Alonso, A., Logan, R., Grodstein, F., Michels, K. B., Willett, W. C., Manson, J. E., & Robins, J. M. (2008). Specifying a target trial prevents immortal time bias and other self-inflicted injuries in observational analyses. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 61(1), 41–45. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2007.03.014
Summary: Outlines the target trial framework, showing how explicitly defining trial components prevents immortal time bias.
Questions:

What is immortal time bias, and how does a target trial prevent it?

What are the seven key components of a target trial protocol?

How does target trial emulation improve transparency?

title: Introduction to Causal Inference & the Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
Why Causality?
Correlation is not causation.
We ask: Does X cause Y?
Examples:

Does ☕ coffee cause longer life?
Does 💊 a drug lower blood pressure?
Does 📚 tutoring improve exam scores?
Does 💵 raising the minimum wage increase unemployment?

title: Introduction to Causal Inference & the Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
Motivating Cases

Medicine: New drug → blood pressure?

Education: Tutoring → exam scores?

Economics: Minimum wage → unemployment?

👉 What kind of study would convince you?

title: Introduction to Causal Inference & the Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
Potential Outcomes Framework
For each unit \(i\):

\(Y_i^{(1)}\): Outcome if treated

\(Y_i^{(0)}\): Outcome if not treated

Individual causal effect:
\[\tau_i = Y_i^{(1)} - Y_i^{(0)}\]

title: Introduction to Causal Inference & the Potential Outcomes Framework
text:
Concept Check 1
Which statement is true?
A. We can always observe both \(Y^{(1)}\) and \(Y^{(0)}\).
B. The causal effect is \(Y^{(1)} + Y^{(0)}\).

title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference
text:
Course Overview
This graduate-level seminar introduces the theory and application of causal inference, with a strong emphasis on biostatistical and epidemiological contexts. The course builds from conceptual foundations and core assumptions to modern estimation methods for causal effects, emphasizing target trial emulation as a unifying framework.
Key frameworks and tools include:

Potential Outcomes Framework & SUTVA
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
Propensity Scores, IPW, and Doubly Robust Methods
Instrumental Variables
Mediation Analysis (NDE/NIE)
Marginal Structural Models (MSMs)
Sensitivity Analysis


Instructor’s Approach
Causal inference is not just a toolbox—it’s a rigorous way of thinking about cause and effect. We will prioritize:

Precise causal questions (not just statistical associations).
Transparency of assumptions (via DAGs and formal notation).
Identification before estimation (thinking carefully about what is learnable from data).
Critical robustness assessment (sensitivity, replication, target trial framing).

title: STAT 579: Applied Causal Inference
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Formulate and distinguish causal from associational questions.
Represent assumptions using DAGs and counterfactual notation.
Evaluate and apply key assumptions (SUTVA, exchangeability, positivity).
Implement modern causal inference methods (propensity scores, IPW, MSMs, IVs, G-computation).
Decompose effects via mediation analysis.
Conduct sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.
Frame observational studies as target trial emulations.
Critically evaluate causal claims in the literature.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
text:
Welcome to Week 4. In our last session, we established a formal definition of confounding and introduced the backdoor criterion as our primary tool for identifying causal effects by conditioning on a sufficient set of covariates. The central lesson was that to estimate the causal effect of an exposure \(A\) on an outcome \(Y\), we must block all non-causal paths between them.
This week, we confront a critical and counter-intuitive reality: conditioning on variables is not always helpful. In fact, conditioning on the wrong variables can introduce bias where none existed. We will explore two major types of “bad controls”:

Mediators: Variables that lie on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome.
Colliders: Variables that are a common effect of the exposure and the outcome (or their ancestors).

The second half of our week is dedicated to selection bias. We will treat it not as a separate, unrelated problem, but as a special, and very common, case of collider-stratification bias. This powerful insight, articulated clearly in Hernán & Robins (2020), allows us to use the same graphical tool—the DAG—to diagnose and reason about confounding and selection bias simultaneously.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
text:
The Problem with “Controlling for Everything”
A common, but misguided, impulse in observational research is to include every available pre-treatment covariate in a regression model. This is sometimes called the “Table 2 Fallacy” or “kitchen sink” regression. The hope is that by conditioning on a rich set of variables, we are more likely to have satisfied the backdoor criterion and controlled for confounding.
However, causal inference is not about blind adjustment; it’s about principled adjustment guided by a causal model. A variable’s role in a causal system determines whether we should condition on it. As we will see, conditioning on the wrong variables is as damaging as failing to condition on the right ones.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
section: “Bad Controls”: Why More Adjustment Isn’t Always Better
text:
“Bad Controls”: Why More Adjustment Isn’t Always Better
A “bad control” is any variable that, when conditioned on, either introduces bias or blocks a causal path of interest. We will focus on the two most important types: mediators and colliders.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
text:
Mediators: Blocking the Causal Path
A mediator (or intermediate variable) is a variable that lies on the causal pathway from the exposure \(A\) to the outcome \(Y\). The causal structure is \(A \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\).

Total Causal Effect: The overall effect of \(A\) on \(Y\) is the sum of its direct effect (\(A \rightarrow Y\)) and its indirect effect (\(A \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\)).
The Problem with Adjustment: When we condition on a mediator \(M\), we block the indirect causal path. The resulting estimate is only for the direct effect of \(A\) on \(Y\). If our research question is about the total effect of the exposure, then adjusting for a mediator will bias our estimate.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
section: Example: Aspirin, Blood Clotting, and Heart Attacks
text:
Example: Aspirin, Blood Clotting, and Heart Attacks
Suppose we want to estimate the total effect of taking aspirin (\(A\)) on the risk of a heart attack (\(Y\)). A primary mechanism by which aspirin works is by reducing blood clotting (\(M\)).
The DAG is: Aspirin \(\rightarrow\) Blood Clotting \(\rightarrow\) Heart Attack.
If we run a regression of Heart Attack ~ Aspirin + Blood Clotting, we are asking: “What is the effect of Aspirin on heart attack risk among people with the same level of blood clotting?” This effectively removes the very pathway through which aspirin has its intended effect. Our estimate for Aspirin would be biased towards the null, reflecting only any other potential non-clotting-related mechanisms.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
text:
Colliders: Creating Spurious Associations
A collider is a variable that is a common effect of two other variables. In the context of a DAG with exposure \(A\) and outcome \(Y\), a variable \(C\) is a collider if the path is \(A \rightarrow C \leftarrow Y\).
This is the most dangerous and counter-intuitive structure in causal inference.

Unconditionally Independent: If two variables \(A\) and \(Y\) are marginally independent (no path between them), they are unassociated.
Conditionally Dependent: Conditioning on a collider opens the path between its causes. It creates a spurious, non-causal association between \(A\) and \(Y\) where none existed before.

This phenomenon is often called collider-stratification bias or endogenous selection bias.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
section: Selection Bias as a Special Case of Collider Bias
text:
Selection Bias as a Special Case of Collider Bias
The insight that selection bias is simply collider bias is one of the most unifying concepts in modern epidemiology (Hernán & Robins (2020), Ch. 8). We can represent the mechanism of selection into our study with a special node, \(S\). Typically, \(S=1\) means an individual is included in the analysis, and \(S=0\) means they are not.
Selection bias occurs whenever we condition on a collider, and our analysis sample is, by definition, conditioned on \(S=1\).
Therefore, selection bias is present if our selection variable \(S\) is a collider on a path between \(A\) and \(Y\) (or their ancestors).

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
text:
Classic Examples of Selection Bias

Berkson’s Paradox (Hospital-based studies): Suppose we are studying the relationship between two independent diseases, say diabetes (\(A\)) and cholecystitis (\(Y\)), using a hospital dataset. A patient is likely to be hospitalized (\(S=1\)) if they have diabetes, or if they have cholecystitis, or both.

DAG: Diabetes \(\rightarrow\) Hospitalization \(\leftarrow\) Cholecystitis.
Bias: Hospitalization (\(S\)) is a collider. In the general population, the two diseases are unassociated. But among hospitalized patients, knowing a patient has diabetes makes it less likely they have cholecystitis to explain their hospitalization. Conditioning on \(S=1\) creates a spurious inverse association.

Loss to Follow-up (Cohort Studies): We are studying the effect of a toxic exposure (\(A\)) on mortality (\(Y\)). The study requires yearly follow-up visits. Suppose the exposure itself causes side effects that make people more likely to drop out of the study (\(A \rightarrow S=0\)). Also suppose that people who are becoming sicker (a precursor to \(Y\)) are also more likely to miss visits and drop out (\(Y \leftarrow U \rightarrow S=0\), where \(U\) is health status).

DAG: \(A \rightarrow S \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\). (Here we model remaining in the study, S, being caused by treatment and health status).
Bias: Remaining in the study (\(S=1\)) is a collider. By analyzing only the subjects who complete the study, we condition on this collider, inducing a spurious association between \(A\) and \(Y\).

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
section: Analogy: The Sprinkler, Rain, and Wet Grass
text:
Analogy: The Sprinkler, Rain, and Wet Grass
This is a classic analogy from Pearl (2009) used to understand colliders.

Let \(A\) = The sprinkler is on.
Let \(Y\) = It is raining.
Let \(C\) = The grass is wet.

The causal structure is: Sprinkler \(\rightarrow\) Wet Grass \(\leftarrow\) Rain.
“Wet Grass” is a collider.

Unconditionally: In general, knowing the sprinkler is on tells you nothing about whether it’s raining. \(A\) and \(Y\) are independent.
Conditionally: Suppose you look outside and see the grass is wet (\(C=1\)). Now, if you also learn that the sprinkler is on (\(A=1\)), you would rightly conclude that it is probably not raining (\(Y=0\)). The two independent causes have become conditionally dependent (in this case, negatively correlated) once we know their common effect.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
section: Confounder vs. Collider: The Golden Rule of Adjustment
text:
Confounder vs. Collider: The Golden Rule of Adjustment
The most critical distinction to master is between a confounder and a collider.








Feature
Confounder (\(L\))
Collider (\(C\))




Visual (DAG)
A common cause: \(A \leftarrow L \rightarrow Y\)
A common effect: \(A \rightarrow C \leftarrow Y\)


Path Type
Creates a “backdoor” non-causal path.
Is the endpoint of a “v-structure”.


Bias
Causes bias if left unadjusted.
Creates bias if adjusted for.


Action
Adjust for it to block the backdoor path.
Do NOT adjust for it. Leave it alone.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
text:
Demonstrating Collider Bias by Hand
Let’s prove numerically that conditioning on a collider induces an association.
Suppose we have a population of 1000 people. We are interested in a gene (\(A\)) and a behavior (\(Y\)), which are, in this hypothetical world, completely independent. Let’s say a person can either have the gene (\(A=1\)) or not (\(A=0\)), and they can either engage in the behavior (\(Y=1\)) or not (\(Y=0\)).

Prevalence of Gene: \(P(A=1) = 0.5\)
Prevalence of Behavior: \(P(Y=1) = 0.5\)
Because they are independent, the joint probability is just the product: \(P(A=1, Y=1) = P(A=1) \times P(Y=1) = 0.25\).

Now, let’s introduce a collider, \(C\), which is “being selected into a special study.” The study only recruits people who have either the gene or the behavior. So, \(C=1\) if \(A=1\) or \(Y=1\).
Let’s build a table for our population of 1000:









Gene (A)
Behavior (Y)
Number of People (Total Pop)
Selected into Study (C=1)?

\(1000 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 250\)

\(1000 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 250\)

\(1000 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 250\)

\(1000 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 250\)
Yes



Step 1: Check for association in the full population. The risk of the behavior (\(Y=1\)) among those without the gene (\(A=0\)) is: \(P(Y=1 | A=0) = \frac{N(A=0, Y=1)}{N(A=0)} = \frac{250}{250+250} = 0.5\) The risk of the behavior (\(Y=1\)) among those with the gene (\(A=1\)) is: \(P(Y=1 | A=1) = \frac{N(A=1, Y=1)}{N(A=1)} = \frac{250}{250+250} = 0.5\) The risks are identical. As designed, there is no association between A and Y in the full population.
Step 2: Check for association within the study sample (i.e., conditional on C=1). Our study sample consists of the 750 people for whom \(C=1\).

Among those in the study who do NOT have the gene (\(A=0\)), all 250 of them MUST have the behavior (\(Y=1\)). \(P(Y=1 | A=0, C=1) = \frac{N(A=0, Y=1, C=1)}{N(A=0, C=1)} = \frac{250}{250} = 1.0\)
Among those in the study who DO have the gene (\(A=1\)), some have the behavior (\(Y=1\)) and some don’t (\(Y=0\)). The total number of people with the gene in the study is \(250+250=500\). \(P(Y=1 | A=1, C=1) = \frac{N(A=1, Y=1, C=1)}{N(A=1, C=1)} = \frac{250}{500} = 0.5\)

The risks are now completely different (1.0 vs 0.5)! By restricting our analysis to the study sample, we have created a spurious negative association. It looks like having the gene is “protective” against the behavior, which is false. This is collider bias.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
section: Visualizing Causal Structures with dagitty and tikz
text:
Visualizing Causal Structures with dagitty and tikz
First, let’s visualize the three key structures: confounder, mediator, and collider.

Code
# Confounder
plot(dagitty("dag { L -> A -> Y; L -> Y }"))

# Mediator
plot(dagitty("dag { A -> M -> Y }"))

# Collider
plot(dagitty("dag { A -> C <- Y }"))












(a) Confounder (Common Cause)











(b) Mediator (Causal Pathway)











(c) Collider (Common Effect)







Figure 1: DAGs for Confounding, Mediation, and Collider Structures

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
text:
Simulating and Identifying Collider Bias
Let’s replicate our hand-calculation example in R. We’ll simulate data where an exposure A and outcome Y are independent, but both cause a third variable, C.


Code
set.seed(123)
n <- 10000
# A and Y are independent standard normal variables
df <- tibble(
  A = rnorm(n),
  Y = rnorm(n)
)

# C is a collider, caused by both A and Y
df <- df |>
  mutate(C = 0.8 * A + 0.8 * Y + rnorm(n))

# Model 1: The correct model (no adjustment)
# We regress Y on A. The coefficient should be near 0.
m1 <- lm(Y ~ A, data = df)

# Model 2: The incorrect model (adjusting for collider C)
# We regress Y on A, but control for C. This will induce bias.
m2 <- lm(Y ~ A + C, data = df)

# Tidy the results into a table
bind_rows(
  tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(Model = "Correct: Y ~ A"),
  tidy(m2, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(Model = "Incorrect: Y ~ A + C")
) |>
  filter(term == "A") |>
  select(Model, term, estimate, p.value, conf.low, conf.high) |>
  kable(
    caption = "Comparing Models With and Without Collider Adjustment",
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Model Specification",
      "Term",
      "Estimate",
      "P-value",
      "2.5%",
      "97.5%"
    )
  )

Interpretation: As you can see from the table, in the correct model (Y ~ A), the coefficient for A is very close to zero and the p-value is large. This correctly reflects our data generating process where A and Y are independent.
However, in the incorrect model where we foolishly “control for” the collider C, the coefficient for A becomes -0.47 with a tiny p-value. The model has manufactured a strong, spurious negative association. This demonstrates that adjusting for a collider is a critical error that can lead to completely wrong conclusions.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
text:
Diagnosing Paths with dagitty
The dagitty package is more than just a plotting tool; it’s an analysis engine. We can ask it to identify adjustment sets.


Code
# Define the collider DAG
collider_dag <- dagitty("dag{ A -> C <- Y }")

# What paths exist between A and Y?
paths(collider_dag, from = "A", to = "Y")


$paths
[1] "A -> C <- Y"

$open
[1] FALSE


The output shows paths: 0, meaning there are no open paths between A and Y. They are d-separated.
Now, what happens if we condition on C?


Code
# Check paths when conditioning on C
paths(collider_dag, from = "A", to = "Y", Z = "C")


$paths
[1] "A -> C <- Y"

$open
[1] TRUE


dagitty confirms that conditioning on C opens the path A -> C <- Y. This is the formal representation of collider bias.

title: Confounding and Selection Bias
section: Lab: The Weight Loss App Paradox
text:
Lab: The Weight Loss App Paradox
Purpose: This lab is designed to give you hands-on experience with identifying and simulating selection bias. You will see how restricting your dataset to a non-random subset of the population can severely bias your results.
Lab Objectives:

Draw a DAG to represent a realistic selection bias scenario.
Write R code to simulate data based on your DAG.
Compare the results of an analysis on the full population versus the selected sub-population.
Interpret the difference and articulate the causal mechanism of the bias.

Scenario: A tech company has developed a new smartphone app (\(A\)) designed to promote weight loss (\(Y\)). They provide you with a dataset to evaluate its effectiveness. The exposure, \(A\), is whether a user was randomly encouraged to use a new, enhanced feature set (\(A=1\)) versus the standard app (\(A=0\)). The outcome, \(Y\), is weight loss in kg after 6 months.

text:
Task 4: Reflection and Interpretation
Instructions: Look at the table from Task 3. Answer the following questions.

What is the estimated effect of the app in the full population? How does this compare to the true effect we specified in the simulation?
What is the estimated effect of the app in the selected sample? Is it close to the true effect?
What is the direction of the bias (i.e., did selection make the app look more or less effective)?
In plain language, explain why the estimate from the selected sample is biased. What non-causal association was created by only looking at active users?

<details>
<summary>Solution to Reflection</summary>

The estimated effect in the full population is ~2.03. This is very close to the true effect of 2.0 we built into our simulation. Because \(A\) was randomized, a simple comparison gives the right answer.
The estimated effect in the selected sample is ~1.44. This is substantially lower than the true effect.
The bias is negative or towards the null. Selection bias made the app appear less effective than it truly is.
The estimate is biased because we conditioned on a collider (\(S\)). In this group of “active users,” a spurious association is created. Think about it: among active users (\(S=1\)), if someone in the standard app group (\(A=0\)) is still active, they must have had very high initial motivation (\(U\)) or been getting unusually good results for other reasons. Conversely, someone in the enhanced app group (\(A=1\)) might remain active even with lower motivation because the app itself is more engaging. This creates a situation where, within the selected group, those with \(A=0\) have, on average, higher values of unmeasured positive factors (\(U\)) than those with \(A=1\). This makes the \(A=0\) group’s outcomes look better than they should, biasing the estimated effect of \(A\) downwards.

</details>

title: Propensity Score Methods
text:
In a perfect world, we would answer all causal questions using a Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). By randomly assigning treatment, we ensure that, on average, the treated and control groups are identical on all background characteristics (both observed and unobserved). Any difference in their outcomes can therefore be attributed to the treatment.
However, in public health and clinical research, RCTs are often unethical, impractical, or too expensive. We must rely on observational data, where individuals select their own treatments. This leads to a critical problem: people who choose treatment are often systematically different from those who do not.
This week, we introduce propensity score methods, a powerful toolkit designed to address this selection bias. Propensity scores allow us to mimic the properties of an RCT by creating balanced comparison groups, helping us to isolate the causal effect of a treatment from the confounding effects of other variables.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define the propensity score and explain its central role in causal inference.
Understand and explain the balancing property of the propensity score and why it is crucial for creating comparable groups.
Estimate propensity scores using logistic regression and other methods.
Implement three core propensity score methods: matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and stratification.
Assess whether a propensity score model has successfully balanced the covariates between the treated and control groups using diagnostic plots and tables.
Critically evaluate the advantages and limitations of propensity score methods and their underlying assumptions.

title: Propensity Score Methods
section: 🧠 Key Concepts: The Why and How of Propensity Scores
text:
🧠 Key Concepts: The Why and How of Propensity Scores

The Fundamental Problem: Apples and Oranges 🍎🍊
Imagine we want to know the effect of a new fitness program (treatment A=1) on weight loss (outcome Y). In our observational data, people who joined the program lost more weight. But can we conclude the program caused the weight loss?
Probably not. The people who chose to join are likely different. They might be younger, more health-conscious, or have better access to healthy food. This is confounding. We are comparing a group of motivated “apples” to a general population of “oranges.”
The goal of propensity scores is to solve this problem by creating a “handicap” system. Instead of trying to match people on dozens of characteristics (age, gender, income, diet, etc.), we can boil all of that information down into a single number: the propensity score.


What is a Propensity Score?

The propensity score is the probability that a unit (e.g., a person) receives the treatment, given their observed baseline covariates.

\[
e(X_i) = P(A_i = 1 | X_i)
\]
Where:

\(A_i = 1\) if person i receives the treatment.
\(X_i\) is the vector of all observed pre-treatment covariates for person i (e.g., age, gender, baseline health status).

Think of it like this: if someone has a propensity score of 0.8, it means that based on their observed characteristics, they had an 80% chance of being in the treatment group. A person with a score of 0.1 had only a 10% chance.


The Magic: The Balancing Property of the Propensity Score
This is the theoretical cornerstone that makes propensity scores so powerful.

Theorem (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983): If we correctly specify the propensity score model, then within strata of the propensity score, the distribution of the observed covariates X is independent of treatment status A.

\[
(Y^1, Y^0) \perp A | X \implies (Y^1, Y^0) \perp A | e(X)
\]
In plain language: If you take a treated person and an untreated person who have the exact same propensity score, you can think of them as being “statistically equivalent” on all the observed covariates that went into the score. It’s as if, for that pair of individuals, the treatment was randomly assigned. By conditioning on this single score, we have “balanced” all the observed confounders simultaneously.






TipKey Assumption: Ignorability & Positivity




Ignorability (or Unconfoundedness): We must assume that we have measured and included all common causes of the treatment and the outcome in our propensity score model. Propensity scores cannot balance unobserved confounders (e.g., genetic factors, motivation).
Positivity (or Overlap): For any set of covariates X, there must be a non-zero probability of being both treated and untreated. \(0 < P(A=1 | X=x) < 1\). If a certain type of person always gets the treatment, we have no one to compare them to.
