title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: The Scenario: Managing High Blood Pressure
text:
The Scenario: Managing High Blood Pressure
Imagine a doctor treating a patient for high blood pressure over several months.

Time-Varying Treatment: The doctor can change the dosage of blood pressure medication at each visit. This is a “time-varying treatment” because it’s not a one-time decision.
Time-Varying Confounder: The patient’s blood pressure reading itself. It changes from visit to visit.
Outcome: The ultimate goal is to prevent a heart attack.

Here’s where the problem, known as treatment-confounder feedback, comes in.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
The Feedback Loop 🔄
This situation creates a tricky chicken-and-egg loop that makes it very difficult to figure out if the medication is truly working.

Treatment Affects the Confounder: The medication you take today directly impacts your blood pressure reading at your next visit. If you take a high dose, your blood pressure will likely be lower next month.

Medication Dose (Today) \(\rightarrow\) Blood Pressure (Next Month)

Confounder Affects the Treatment: When the doctor sees your lower blood pressure next month, they will use that information to decide on your next dose. Seeing a good reading, they might keep the dose the same or even lower it.

Blood Pressure (Next Month) \(\rightarrow\) Medication Dose (Next Month)


This loop is problematic because the variable we need to “control for” (blood pressure) is also something we are trying to change with our treatment. The blood pressure reading is both a confounder for the next treatment decision and a mediator of the last treatment’s effect.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Why Standard Statistical Methods Fail
Normally, to isolate a treatment’s effect, a statistician would try to “adjust for” or “control for” the confounder. In this case, that would mean trying to answer the question: “Holding blood pressure constant, what is the effect of the medication?”

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: This is the Wrong Question to Ask, and here’s why
text:
This is the Wrong Question to Ask, and here’s why
Imagine you’re trying to figure out if a new fertilizer makes plants grow taller. The fertilizer works by helping the plant build a stronger stem, which then allows it to grow. The stem’s strength is part of the causal pathway.
If you try to “control for” the stem’s strength, you are essentially asking: “For plants with the exact same stem strength, which one grew taller?” This question is nonsensical. You’ve just eliminated the very mechanism through which the fertilizer works! You’ve blocked the causal path.
It’s the same with the blood pressure medication. The medication works by lowering blood pressure. If we statistically “hold blood pressure constant,” we block the main pathway of the drug’s effect. Doing so makes the medication look ineffective, even if it’s saving lives.
This is the fundamental challenge: the confounder isn’t just a nuisance variable to be adjusted away; it is a key piece of the causal story that is directly influenced by what we did in the past. Standard methods can’t untangle this feedback loop, which is why specialized techniques like Marginal Structural Models (MSMs) were invented.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
How it Works
We left off with our doctor, who is stuck in a feedback loop: the medication dose affects the patient’s blood pressure, and the blood pressure then affects the next medication dose. We can’t just “control for” blood pressure because that would block the very effect we want to measure.
So, how do Marginal Structural Models (MSMs) solve this puzzle?
The big idea is this: Instead of trying to statistically adjust for blood pressure, we create a new, imaginary version of our dataset where the feedback loop never existed in the first place.
We do this using a powerful technique called Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW). Here’s the intuition.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Creating a “Fair” Comparison with Weights
Imagine in our study, we have two patients with dangerously high blood pressure.

Patient A is given a high dose of medication. This is the expected decision. The doctor saw the high blood pressure and acted accordingly.
Patient B, for some unusual reason, is given a low dose of medication. This is a surprising decision. It goes against what the doctor would normally do.

Patient B is incredibly valuable to us. They are a rare example of someone who breaks the feedback loop. They show us what happens when a high-risk person gets a low dose. Because they are so rare and informative, we want to give their outcome more weight in our analysis.
Conversely, Patient A’s outcome is less informative. They are just one of many high-risk patients who got the expected high dose. So, we give their outcome less weight.
MSMs do this systematically for every patient at every visit. Each person is given a statistical “weight” based on the treatment they received.

If the treatment was surprising (like getting a low dose despite high blood pressure), the patient gets a large weight.
If the treatment was expected (like getting a high dose for high blood pressure), the patient gets a small weight.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
The Magic of the “Pseudo-Population”
After calculating these weights for everyone, we have essentially created a new, weighted dataset. We call this a pseudo-population.
In this new, imaginary population, something amazing has happened: the link between blood pressure and the medication dose has been statistically erased. It’s as if we’ve created a parallel universe where the doctor made treatment decisions at random, without ever looking at the patient’s blood pressure readings.
Because the confounding from the feedback loop is now gone, we have simulated a perfect randomized controlled trial.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
The Final, Simple Step
Once we have this “fair” pseudo-population, the final analysis is incredibly simple. We no longer need to worry about adjusting for blood pressure. We can now directly and fairly compare the long-term outcomes (like heart attacks) of patients who followed a strategy of “always take a high dose” versus those who followed a strategy of “always take a low dose.”
In short, MSMs solve the feedback problem not by trying to adjust for the time-varying confounder, but by re-weighting the entire study population to create a new dataset where the confounding doesn’t exist. It’s a clever way to simulate the ideal experiment that we couldn’t run in real life.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: From a Biased Sample to a Fair Representation
text:
From a Biased Sample to a Fair Representation
Think about a national political poll. If a pollster only calls people from one state, say California, their results won’t represent the entire country. The sample is biased. To fix this, pollsters use weights. If they have too few respondents from Texas, they give each Texan’s answer a little more weight. If they have too many from California, they give each Californian’s answer a little less weight. By doing this, they create a weighted sample that statistically mirrors the entire country.
The pseudo-population in an MSM works on the exact same principle.

Our Real-World Data (The Biased Sample): Our observational study is like the biased poll. It’s biased because the doctor’s decisions weren’t random. Patients with high blood pressure were far more likely to get high-dose medication. The “surprising” patients (high blood pressure, low dose) are like the under-sampled Texans—they are rare but crucial.
The Weights (The Correction Factor): The Inverse Probability Weights are the correction factors. We give a large weight to the “surprising” patients and a small weight to the “expected” patients.
The Pseudo-Population (The Fair Representation): When we apply these weights, we generate our pseudo-population. This new, imaginary dataset is no longer biased. It now represents a world where the treatment decisions were fair and unbiased.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
What Does “Statistically Erased” Mean?
Let’s make this concrete. Imagine we look at just the patients in our study who had high blood pressure at their second visit.

In the REAL data, the table might look like this:




Patient’s Blood Pressure
Medication Dose
Number of Patients




High
High Dose
90


High
Low Dose
10



You can see the bias immediately. For high-risk patients, there’s a 90% chance they get a high dose. The link between blood pressure and treatment is strong.

In the PSEUDO-POPULATION, after weighting, it looks like this:









Patient’s Blood Pressure
Medication Dose
Weighted Number of Patients




High
High Dose
50


High
Low Dose
50



The magic is that the total number of patients is still the same, but their influence has been redistributed. The 10 “surprising” patients who got a low dose now have such a large weight that they count for as much as the 90 “expected” patients.
Within the group of high-risk patients, the treatment is now perfectly balanced—50/50. The arrow from “Blood Pressure” to “Medication Dose” has been statistically erased. We’ve created a dataset where it appears the doctor just flipped a coin to decide the dose, which is exactly what happens in a randomized controlled trial.
That’s the essence of the pseudo-population: it’s a carefully re-weighted version of our real data that mathematically undoes the biases of real-world decision-making, allowing us to ask our causal question fairly.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: Scaffolding the Core Idea: Probability and Its Inverse
text:
Scaffolding the Core Idea: Probability and Its Inverse
At its heart, the weight is just the number one divided by a probability.
\[
W = \frac{1}{\text{Probability}}
\tag{1}\]
The whole point is to give more influence to things that were unlikely to happen, and less influence to things that were likely.

If an event had a low probability (it was surprising), its inverse is a big number.

Example: Probability = 10% or 0.10. The weight is 1 / 0.10 = 10.

If an event had a high probability (it was expected), its inverse is a small number.

Example: Probability = 80% or 0.80. The weight is 1 / 0.80 = 1.25.


Think of it like this: if you find a rare Pokémon card (a low probability event), it’s worth a lot. If you find a common one (a high probability event), it’s worth very little. The weight represents the “value” or “informativeness” of an observation.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: Building the Math, Step by Step
text:
Building the Math, Step by Step
Let’s get specific. Our goal is to calculate a weight for each person in our study. This weight will depend on the entire sequence of treatments they received over time.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
The Unstabilized Weight (\(W_i\))
First, let’s look at the basic, “unstabilized” weight for a single person, whom we’ll call person i.
The formula for the unstabilized weight is:
\[
W_i = \frac{1}{\prod_{k=0}^{K} \Prob{A_k=A_{i,k} \mid \bar{A}_{i,k-1}, \bar{L}_{i,k}}}
\tag{2}\]
Let’s decode that:

\(A_{i,k}\): The actual treatment person i received at time \(k\).
\(\bar{A}_{i,k-1}\): The person’s entire history of treatment before time \(k\).
\(\bar{L}_{i,k}\): The person’s entire history of confounders up to and including time \(k\).
\(\Prob{\cdot}\): This is the probability of receiving their actual treatment, given their specific history. We get this from a statistical model (like logistic regression).
\(\prod_{k=0}^{K}\): This is the “product” symbol. It means we multiply the probabilities from each time point together (from the start of the study, \(k=0\), to the end, \(k=K\)).







Note



In plain English: For each person, we calculate the probability of them getting the treatment they got at each visit, given their past. Then we multiply all those probabilities together. The final weight is just 1 divided by that result.








TipThe Denominator is “The Story of What Happened”



Think of the denominator as telling the story of why the doctor made the decisions they did. It’s the probability of the observed treatment sequence, fully explained by the patient’s entire medical history.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
The Stabilized Weight (\(SW_i\))
Unstabilized weights work, but they can sometimes become huge, making our results unstable. To fix this, we use “stabilized” weights, which are much better behaved.
The formula for the stabilized weight is:
\[
SW_i = \prod_{k=0}^{K} \frac{\Prob{A_k=A_{i,k} \mid \bar{A}_{i, k-1}}}{\Prob{A_k=A_{i,k} \mid \bar{A}_{i, k-1}, \bar{L}_{i,k}}}
\tag{3}\]
This looks more complex, but it’s a simple, brilliant tweak.

The denominator is the same as before. It’s the probability of the treatment given the full history (treatments and confounders).
The numerator is new. It’s the probability of receiving the treatment given only the past treatment history, ignoring the confounders (\(\bar{L}\)).

In plain English: The stabilized weight is a ratio. For each time point, we ask:

What was the chance of this treatment, given only past treatments? (Numerator)
What was the chance of this treatment, given the full medical history? (Denominator)

We calculate this fraction for every time point and multiply them all together. This process “stabilizes” the weights by preventing them from getting too large.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: A Simple Numerical Example by Hand
text:
A Simple Numerical Example by Hand
Let’s use our tiny 5-patient dataset from the lecture. We will calculate the stabilized weight for Patient.
Patient 4’s History:

Time 0: Was Treated (\(A_0 = 1\))
Time 1: Had a good biomarker result (\(L_1=0\)) and was Treated (\(A_1=1\)). The formula for their weight is:

\[
SW_4 = \left( \frac{\Prob{A_0=1}}{\Prob{A_0=1}} \right) \times \left( \frac{\Prob{A_1=1 \mid A_0=1}}{\Prob{A_1=1 \mid A_0=1, L_1=0}} \right)
\]
Step 1: Calculate the needed probabilities from the data.
(These are the same probabilities we calculated in the lecture.)

For the Numerator:

\(\Prob{A_0=1}\): 3 out of 5 patients were treated at Time 0. So, the probability is 0.6.
\(\Prob{A_1=1 \mid A_0=1}\): Of the 3 patients who got treated at Time 0 (IDs 3, 4, 5), 2 of them were treated at Time 1 (IDs 4, 5). So, the probability is 2/3.

For the Denominator:

\(\Prob{A_0=1}\): Same as above, 0.6. (There are no past confounders L_0 to worry about).
\(\Prob{A_1=1 \mid A_0=1, L_1=0}\): We look only at patients who had \(A_0=1\) and \(L_1=0\) (IDs 3, 4). Of these 2 patients, 1 was treated at Time 1 (ID 4). So, the probability is 1/2 or 0.5. Step 2: Plug the numbers into the formula.

For Time 0: The fraction is \(\frac{0.6}{0.6} = 1\).
For Time 1: The fraction is \(\frac{2/3}{1/2} = \frac{0.667}{0.5} \approx 1.33\). Step 3: Multiply the results together.

\[
SW_4 = 1 \times 1.33 = \mathbf{1.33}
\]
This is the stabilized weight for Patient 4. We are giving them slightly more weight in our pseudo-population. Why? Because getting treated at Time 1 was only a 50/50 chance for people with their specific history (\(A_0=1\), \(L_1=0\)). It wasn’t a “sure thing,” so their outcome is more informative than someone whose treatment was 100% predictable.

❓ Check Your Understanding
Now, try it yourself! Using the same logic and the probabilities from our example, calculate the stabilized weight for Patient.

Patient’s History: Was Untreated (\(A_0=0\)), had a bad biomarker (\(L_1=1\)), and was then Treated (\(A_1=1\)).



Click for a step-by-step solution.


Set up the formula for Patient #2: \[
SW_2 = \left( \frac{\Prob{A_0=0}}{\Prob{A_0=0}} \right) \times \left( \frac{\Prob{A_1=1 \mid A_0=0}}{\Prob{A_1=1 \mid A_0=0, L_1=1}} \right)
\]
Find the probabilities:


Numerator:

\(\Prob{A_0=0} = 2/5 = 0.4\)
\(\Prob{A_1=1 \mid A_0=0}\): Look at patients with \(A_0=0\) (IDs 1, 2). One of them got$ A_1=1$ (ID 2). So, probability = 1/2 or 0.5.

Denominator: *\(\Prob{A_0=0} = 0.4\)

\(\Prob{A_1=1 \mid A_0=0, L_1=1}\): Look at patients with \(A_0=0\) and \(L_1=1\) (only ID 2). That one patient got \(A_1=1\). So, probability = 1/1 or 1.0.



Plug and solve: \[
SW_2 = \left( \frac{0.4}{0.4} \right) \times \left( \frac{0.5}{1.0} \right) = 1 \times 0.5 = \mathbf{0.5}
\]

Meaning: We give Patient #2 less weight. Why? Because their treatment at Time 1 was completely predictable. For every patient with their history, the doctor gave them the treatment. Their outcome is less surprising and thus less informative for breaking the feedback loop.


This mathematical process of weighting is how we build the pseudo-population. By carefully adjusting the “influence” of each person, we create a new, balanced dataset where the link between confounders and treatments is broken, allowing for a fair causal comparison.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Assumptions
The mathematical “magic” of creating a pseudo-population is powerful, but it’s not infallible. It rests on a few critical assumptions about our data and the world. If these assumptions are violated, our weights will be incorrect and our causal conclusions will be biased.
Let’s go through the three most important assumptions: sequential exchangeability, positivity, and consistency.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: 1. Sequential Exchangeability (No Unmeasured Confounding Over Time)
text:
1. Sequential Exchangeability (No Unmeasured Confounding Over Time)
This is the most important and untestable assumption. It’s the longitudinal version of the standard “exchangeability” or “ignorability” assumption we’ve seen before.
The Core Idea: At every point in time, the reason a person gets a particular treatment must be fully explained by their observed past history—that is, the data we have in our spreadsheet. There can be no hidden or unmeasured factors that influence the treatment decision.
Analogy: The All-Knowing Researcher Imagine you are the researcher, and you are watching our doctor treat the patient with high blood pressure. - Assumption Holds: At each visit, the doctor looks at the patient’s chart—past blood pressure readings, past medication doses, age, etc.—and makes a decision. As long as you have that same chart (all the same data), you can build an accurate model of the doctor’s decision-making. The reason for the treatment is known. - Assumption Violated: What if the doctor also bases their decision on something you can’t see? For example, the doctor might notice “the patient looks especially pale today” or “the patient mentioned feeling dizzy.” If these factors influence the treatment dose but are not recorded in your dataset, you have an unmeasured confounder.
When this happens, your model for the probability of treatment will be wrong because it’s missing a key predictor. The weights you calculate will be incorrect, and the pseudo-population will still be biased.






Important📌 Sequential Exchangeability



Formally, this means that at any time \(k\), the potential outcome \(Y^{\bar{a}}\) is independent of the actual treatment received \(A_k\), conditional on the observed past treatment (\(\bar{A}_{k-1}\)) and confounder (\(\bar{L}_k\)) histories.
\[
Y^{\bar{a}} \indep A_k \mid \bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k
\]
This must hold for all time points \(k\). It is a strong assumption that requires deep subject-matter expertise to justify.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
2. Positivity (Anything Can Happen)
This is a more practical, and in principle, testable assumption.
The Core Idea: For any given patient history, there must be a non-zero probability of receiving either treatment. Treatment decisions cannot be deterministic.
Analogy: The Doctor With No “Never” or “Always” Rules Positivity is violated if our doctor has a strict, unbreakable rule.

Assumption Holds: For every combination of patient history (age, past blood pressure, past medication doses), there is always at least some chance (even if small) that the doctor might choose either a high dose or a low dose. Anything can happen.
Violation Example: Imagine the hospital has a rigid policy: “Any patient whose blood pressure is above 180 mmHg must be given the high dose, no exceptions.”
The Problem: For this group of very sick patients, the probability of receiving the low dose is exactly zero.

Why This Breaks the Math: The weight calculation involves dividing by this probability (\(\text{weight} \approx 1/\text{probability}\)). If the probability is zero, we are trying to divide by zero, which is impossible. The weight becomes infinite, and our analysis fails.
The Practical Meaning: We can’t learn about the effect of a treatment in a certain type of person if no one in that group ever receives it. To learn what happens to very sick patients under a low-dose regimen, we need at least some very sick patients to have actually received the low dose in our study.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: 3. Consistency (What You See Is What You Get)
text:
3. Consistency (What You See Is What You Get)
This assumption connects the data we observe to the causal effects we want to estimate.
The Core Idea: The treatment value in our dataset (e.g., \(A=1\) for “high dose”) must correspond to a clearly defined, real-world intervention. And the outcome we observe for a person who got that intervention must be the same as their potential outcome under that intervention.
Analogy: A Standardized Recipe Imagine “high dose” is our treatment.

Assumption Holds: “High dose” means exactly “50mg of Drug X, taken once daily” for every patient, every time. The intervention is well-defined.
Assumption Violated: What if for some patients, “high dose” meant “50mg of Drug X,” but for others, it meant “50mg of Drug X plus a recommendation to follow a low-salt diet”? In this case, \(A=1\) refers to two different versions of the treatment. If we get a causal effect estimate, we won’t know if it’s due to the drug, the diet, or the combination.

The consistency assumption ensures that we are estimating the effect of a specific, non-ambiguous intervention.
These three assumptions are the theoretical foundation upon which Marginal Structural Models are built. Justifying them is the most important step in any such analysis.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
When Sequential Exchangeability Fails (Unmeasured Confounding)
This is the most difficult violation to handle because you can’t definitively prove it with data. It relies on subject-matter knowledge.
The Problem: You suspect there are important, unmeasured confounders that influenced both treatment and outcome. Your weights are wrong because the model for the denominator is missing key variables.
What to Do:

Think Harder (A Priori): The best “solution” is prevention. Before the study, consult with domain experts to identify and measure all potential confounders. If you are using existing data, try to find proxy variables that might capture some of the unmeasured confounding.
Conduct a Sensitivity Analysis (Post Hoc): Since you can’t measure the unmeasured confounder, the next best thing is to quantify how much it could affect your results.

The Core Idea: A sensitivity analysis asks, “How strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be to change my conclusion?”
Analogy: Stress-Testing a Bridge: Imagine you’ve built a bridge and concluded it’s safe. A sensitivity analysis is like putting it in a wind tunnel. You increase the wind speed until the bridge breaks. This tells you its limits. Similarly, we can calculate how strong the associations between an unmeasured confounder, the treatment, and the outcome would need to be to, for example, make our estimated effect of zero.
The Result: You can then make a statement like, “Our finding that the drug is effective would be overturned only if there were an unmeasured confounder that was three times more prevalent in the treated group and increased the risk of the outcome by 300%—a confounder far stronger than any known risk factor.” This provides a quantitative measure of how robust your conclusion is.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
When Positivity Fails (Deterministic Treatment)
This violation is often detectable in your data and is a common issue in practice.
The Problem: You have subgroups of people who, given their history, had a 0% or 100% chance of getting the treatment. This results in infinite or near-infinite weights.
How to Diagnose It: - Examine strata: Look for combinations of covariates where everyone or no one gets the treatment. - Look at your weights: This is the most common method. Plot a histogram of your calculated stabilized weights (\(SW_i\)). If you see a few weights that are dramatically larger than the rest (e.g., weights of 50, 100, or 1000), you have a practical positivity problem.
What to Do:

Redefine the Target Population: If the positivity violation is confined to a specific, often extreme group (e.g., only the healthiest people always refuse treatment), you can restrict your analysis to the population where positivity holds. The cost is that your conclusion is no longer generalizable to the excluded group. You would state, “Among patients with characteristics X, Y, and Z, the treatment has a causal effect of…”
Weight Truncation (or Trimming): This is a common pragmatic solution. You set an artificial ceiling on the weights. For example, you might decide to cap all weights at the 99th percentile. Any weight that is calculated to be higher than, say, 20, is manually set to 20. This introduces a small amount of bias (because you are altering the weights) but can drastically reduce variance and make your final estimate more stable. It’s a classic bias-variance trade-off.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
When Consistency Fails (Ambiguous Treatment)
This is a conceptual problem that requires you to go back to the study design and data dictionary.
The Problem: The treatment variable in your dataset (\(A=1\)) does not correspond to a single, well-defined intervention.
What to Do:

Specify the Intervention: The best solution is to be more precise. The causal question should be refined. Instead of asking about the effect of “physical therapy,” which could mean many things, you might have to limit your analysis to the effect of “one weekly 60-minute session with a licensed physical therapist following Protocol X.”
Acknowledge Ambiguity: If the different versions of the treatment cannot be disentangled in the data, you must be transparent about this in your interpretation. You are not estimating the effect of one specific intervention, but rather the effect of a policy or strategy where different interventions are grouped under one label. Your conclusion becomes, “We estimated the effect of a policy of prescribing ‘high dose’ therapy, which may have included different specific treatments across individuals.”

Addressing these violations is what makes causal inference a thoughtful blend of statistical modeling and scientific reasoning.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
1. Checking Sequential Exchangeability (No Unmeasured Confounding)
This first assumption is not checked with code, but with your brain and subject-matter expertise.

The Question You Must Ask: “What are the key factors a doctor would consider when deciding to start a patient on AZT at each visit?”
Our Simulated World: In our hiv_data simulation, the decision to start AZT (A0_azt, A1_azt) depended only on the patient’s past AZT use and their CD4 counts (L0_cd4, L1_cd4).
The Check: As long as we have measured past AZT use and CD4 count, the assumption holds in our simulated world. In a real project, you would need to consult with clinicians to ensure you’ve measured all the important factors (e.g., viral load, opportunistic infections, patient-reported symptoms) that guide this decision. This check happens before you run the models.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
2. Checking Positivity (Anything Can Happen)
This is a practical check we perform after calculating the weights. The main tool is to inspect the distribution of the stabilized weights. Extreme weights are a tell-tale sign of a positivity problem.
Step 1: Visualize the Weight Distribution
A simple histogram is the best place to start.


Code
# Load the data and code from the previous lab if you haven't already
# (Code to generate hiv_wide and the 'sw' column)
set.seed(123)
n_lab <- 500
id <- 1:n_lab
cd4_0 <- rnorm(n_lab, 500, 50)
azt_0_prob <- plogis(-8 + (cd4_0 / 50))
azt_0 <- rbinom(n_lab, 1, azt_0_prob)
cd4_1 <- 0.8 * cd4_0 + 20 * azt_0 + rnorm(n_lab, 50, 10)
azt_1_prob <- plogis(-8 + (cd4_1 / 50) + 0.5 * azt_0)
azt_1 <- rbinom(n_lab, 1, azt_1_prob)
cd4_final <- 0.7 * cd4_1 + 40 * azt_1 + 30 * azt_0 + rnorm(n_lab, 100, 20)
hiv_wide <- data.frame(
  id,
  L0_cd4 = cd4_0,
  A0_azt = azt_0,
  L1_cd4 = cd4_1,
  A1_azt = azt_1,
  Y_cd4 = cd4_final
)
den_mod_A0_lab <- glm(A0_azt ~ L0_cd4, data = hiv_wide, family = binomial)
den_mod_A1_lab <- glm(
  A1_azt ~ A0_azt + L0_cd4 + L1_cd4,
  data = hiv_wide,
  family = binomial
)
num_mod_A0_lab <- glm(A0_azt ~ 1, data = hiv_wide, family = binomial)
num_mod_A1_lab <- glm(A1_azt ~ A0_azt, data = hiv_wide, family = binomial)
hiv_wide$pd0 <- predict(den_mod_A0_lab, type = "response")
hiv_wide$pd1 <- predict(den_mod_A1_lab, type = "response")
hiv_wide$pn0 <- predict(num_mod_A0_lab, type = "response")
hiv_wide$pn1 <- predict(num_mod_A1_lab, type = "response")
hiv_wide$sw0 <- ifelse(
  hiv_wide$A0_azt == 1,
  hiv_wide$pn0 / hiv_wide$pd0,
  (1 - hiv_wide$pn0) / (1 - hiv_wide$pd0)
)
hiv_wide$sw1 <- ifelse(
  hiv_wide$A1_azt == 1,
  hiv_wide$pn1 / hiv_wide$pd1,
  (1 - hiv_wide$pn1) / (1 - hiv_wide$pd1)
)
hiv_wide$sw <- hiv_wide$sw0 * hiv_wide$sw1

# Now, let's do the check
hist(
  hiv_wide$sw,
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Distribution of Stabilized Weights",
  xlab = "Weight Value",
  col = "skyblue"
)





Distribution of stabilized weights. Note the long right tail indicating some very large weights.




Interpretation: The histogram shows that most weights are clustered between 0 and 5, which is good. However, there’s a long “tail” to the right, with a few weights stretching out to 20 or more. These extreme values can give a handful of individuals undue influence over our final result. This is a classic sign of a practical positivity violation.
Step 2: Investigate the Extreme Weights
Let’s look at the patients with the largest weights to understand why they are so “surprising.”


Code
# Get a summary of the weights
summary(hiv_wide$sw)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.1090  0.8186  0.9046  1.0010  1.0455  7.5413 


Code
# Look at the top 5 highest weights
hiv_wide |>
  arrange(desc(sw)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, sw, A0_azt, L0_cd4, A1_azt, L1_cd4) |>
  head(5)



  



Interpretation: Look at patient 419. Their weight is 7.54! This person had a very low CD4 count at baseline (L0_cd4), yet they were not treated with AZT (A0_azt = 0). This was a very unlikely event. The model for treatment probability assigned them a very small probability in the denominator, which, when inverted, created a massive weight.
Step 3: Address the Violation with Weight Truncation
The most common solution is to “truncate” or “trim” the weights. We set a ceiling, and any weight that exceeds this ceiling is brought down to the maximum allowed value. A common practice is to truncate at the 1st and 99th percentiles.


Code
# Calculate the 99th percentile of the weights
percentile_99 <- quantile(hiv_wide$sw, 0.99)
print(paste("99th percentile for truncation is:", round(percentile_99, 2)))


[1] "99th percentile for truncation is: 2.61"


Code
# Create a new, truncated weight variable
hiv_wide$sw_trunc <- ifelse(
  hiv_wide$sw > percentile_99,
  percentile_99,
  hiv_wide$sw
)

# Plot the new distribution
hist(
  hiv_wide$sw_trunc,
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Distribution of Truncated Stabilized Weights",
  xlab = "Truncated Weight Value",
  col = "lightgreen"
)









Interpretation: Notice how the new histogram has no extreme tail. We have removed the influence of those few highly unusual individuals. This will make our final model more stable.
Step 4: Rerun the MSM with the Truncated Weights
Now we refit our final model, but we use the new sw_trunc variable in the weights argument.


Code
library(geepack) # Make sure geeglm is available

msm_lab_fit_truncated <- geeglm(
  Y_cd4 ~ A0_azt + A1_azt,
  data = hiv_wide,
  id = id,
  weights = sw_trunc, # Using the truncated weights
  corstr = "independence"
)

summary(msm_lab_fit_truncated)



Call:
geeglm(formula = Y_cd4 ~ A0_azt + A1_azt, data = hiv_wide, weights = sw_trunc, 
    id = id, corstr = "independence")

(Intercept)  409.957   5.427 5706.10   <2e-16 ***
A0_azt        46.617   5.601   69.28   <2e-16 ***
A1_azt        45.194   4.657   94.16   <2e-16 ***
---

Correlation structure = independence

The Takeaway: Compare these results to the ones from the original model. The coefficient estimates may change slightly—this is the bias we introduce by trimming—but the standard errors will often be smaller, reflecting a more stable and precise estimate. This is the bias-variance trade-off in action.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
3. Checking Consistency (Unambiguous Treatment)
Like exchangeability, this is a conceptual check.

The Question You Must Ask: “Does A0_azt = 1 mean the same thing for everyone?”
The Check: This requires you to understand the study protocol. If A0_azt = 1 could mean a 50mg dose for some patients and a 100mg dose for others, or if some also received adherence counseling, then the consistency assumption is violated. Your analysis should be limited to the specific, well-defined treatment that you are interested in.

By systematically walking through these checks, you can build confidence in the validity of your Marginal Structural Model and produce more robust and defensible causal estimates.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: The Rationale: Why “Stabilize” in the First Place?
text:
The Rationale: Why “Stabilize” in the First Place?
The simpler, “unstabilized” weight for a person is calculated as \(W_i = 1 / \Prob{\text{treatment} | \text{full history}}\). This weight does its job of creating a pseudo-population where confounding is removed. However, it can suffer from a serious statistical problem: high variance.
The Problem of Extreme Weights
Imagine a patient who is very healthy, and for healthy patients, the probability of receiving a risky experimental drug is extremely low, say 1 in 1000 (\(\Prob{A=1 | \text{history}} = 0.001\)). If this patient, against all odds, does receive the drug, their unstabilized weight would be: \(W_i = 1 / 0.001 = 1000\)
This means that in our analysis, this single individual has the same influence as 1000 other people. If their outcome is unusual, they alone could dramatically swing the entire study’s conclusion. This makes our results highly unstable and sensitive to a few rare individuals. Our estimate might be unbiased on average, but its variance would be huge, leading to very wide and unreliable confidence intervals.
The Goal of Stabilization: The goal is to create a new set of weights that still correctly adjusts for confounding but doesn’t have this extreme variance. We want to rein in these massive weights without losing the crucial adjustment they provide.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: The Intuition: How the Numerator Fixes the Problem
text:
The Intuition: How the Numerator Fixes the Problem
The stabilized weight formula accomplishes this with a clever tweak:
\[
SW_i = \prod_{k=0}^{K} \frac{\Prob{A_k=A_{i,k} \mid \bar{A}_{i, k-1}} \text{ (The Numerator)}}{\Prob{A_k=A_{i,k} \mid \bar{A}_{i, k-1}, \bar{L}_{i,k}} \text{ (The Denominator)}}
\]
Let’s focus on the role of the new numerator.

The Denominator is the probability of treatment for someone with a specific history (e.g., a 62-year-old male with low blood pressure). This can be very small.
The Numerator is the probability of treatment based only on past treatments, averaged over all possible confounder values. It represents the overall proportion of people who received that treatment at that time. This probability is generally not extreme.

The stabilized weight, therefore, compares the patient-specific probability (denominator) to the overall average probability (numerator).
The numerator acts as a moderating factor. Instead of just inverting the denominator (which can lead to an explosion), we are scaling it relative to a more stable, average probability. This keeps the weights in a much more reasonable range, reducing their variance and making our final estimate more stable and precise.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: Simple Numerical Example: Unstabilized vs. Stabilized
text:
Simple Numerical Example: Unstabilized vs. Stabilized
Let’s make this concrete with a simple, one-time treatment study.
Scenario: We’re testing a new drug (\(A=1\)) against a placebo (\(A=0\)). The key confounder (\(L\)) is the severity of the disease: Mild (\(L=0\)) or Severe (\(L=1\)). Doctors are more likely to give the drug to severe patients.

Drug (\(A=1\))
80



Let’s focus on one specific person: A mild patient who received the drug. This is a “surprising” event.

Step 1: Calculate the Unstabilized Weight (\(W_i\))
The formula is \(W_i = 1 / \Prob{A=1 \mid L=0}\).

\(\Prob{A=1 \mid L=0} = \frac{\text{Mild patients who got Drug}}{\text{All Mild patients}} = \frac{10}{90 + 10} = 0.10\)
\(W_i = 1 / 0.10 = \mathbf{10}\)

This person has the weight of 10 people in the analysis.


Step 2: Calculate the Stabilized Weight (\(SW_i\))
The formula is \(SW_i = \Prob{A=1} / \Prob{A=1 \mid L=0}\).

Denominator: We already have this: \(\Prob{A=1 \mid L=0} = \mathbf{0.10}\).
Numerator: We need the overall probability of getting the drug, regardless of severity.

\(\Prob{A=1} = \frac{\text{Total patients who got Drug}}{\text{All patients}} = \frac{10 + 80}{90 + 10 + 20 + 80} = \frac{90}{200} = \mathbf{0.45}\)

Calculate the weight:

\(SW_i = \frac{\text{Numerator}}{\text{Denominator}} = \frac{0.45}{0.10} = \mathbf{4.5}\)




The Comparison



Weight Type
Calculation
Result




Unstabilized
\(1 / 0.10\)
10


Stabilized
\(0.45 / 0.10\)
4.5



Both weights correctly identify this person as being “surprising” and give them more influence. But the stabilized weight is much less extreme. It has been moderated by the fact that getting the drug wasn’t that rare overall (45% of all patients got it). The weight is pulled back from 10 to a more stable 4.5.
By applying this logic to every person, we get a full set of stabilized weights that successfully adjust for confounding while having much lower variance, leading to more precise and reliable causal effect estimates.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text: More Insight

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: Intuition: what the Numerator is Doing (and why it helps)
text:
Intuition: what the Numerator is Doing (and why it helps)

Unstabilized weights upweight people who received a treatment that was unlikely given their full history (past treatments + covariates). That breaks the dependence between covariates and treatment, but the weights can explode when those probabilities are tiny.
Stabilized weights add a numerator that is the simpler probability of the observed treatment given only past treatment. This:

Cancels the worst denominators just enough to shrink extreme weights.
Preserves the marginal (over covariates) distribution of treatment given past treatment, which keeps the weighted sample looking like the original sample in terms of how often each treatment was used.
Keeps the same causal target. The numerator does not reintroduce confounding; it’s “harmless” for identification but helpful for variance.


Rule of thumb: the numerator reintroduces the right amount of randomness we had in treatment before we looked at covariates, so weights stay near 1 instead of going wild.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: Definitions (one time point First, then many)
text:
Definitions (one time point First, then many)

One time point (for clarity)

Unstabilized weight for person \(i\):

\[
W_i \;=\; \frac{1}{\Pr(A_i=a_i \mid L_i)}
\]

Stabilized weight for person \(i\):

\[
SW_i \;=\; \frac{\Pr(A_i=a_i)}{\Pr(A_i=a_i \mid L_i)}
\]
Here \(A\) is treatment, \(L\) are confounders.


Multiple time Points \(k=0,\dots,K\)

Unstabilized:

\[
W_i \;=\; \prod_{k=0}^{K} \frac{1}{\Pr(A_{ik}=a_{ik}\mid \bar A_{i,k-1}, \bar L_{ik})}
\]

Stabilized (your formula):

\[
SW_i \;=\; \prod_{k=0}^{K}
  \frac{ \Pr(A_{ik}=a_{ik} \mid \bar A_{i,k-1}) }
       { \Pr(A_{ik}=a_{ik} \mid \bar A_{i,k-1}, \bar L_{ik}) }
\]
The denominator is the same as before (the “hard” assignment model that depends on confounders). The numerator is a “reduced” model (ignores \(L\)).

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: 3 Why Stabilized Weights Keep the Target and Reduce variance (a Clean factorization)
text:
3 Why Stabilized Weights Keep the Target and Reduce variance (a Clean factorization)
Let the observed data density factorize by time as usual:
\[
f(\text{data}) \;=\; f(L_0)\;
\prod_{k=0}^{K} f(A_k \mid \bar A_{k-1}, \bar L_k)\, f(L_{k+1}\mid \bar A_k, \bar L_k).
\]
If we reweight each record by
\[
SW \;=\; \prod_{k=0}^{K} \frac{ f(A_k \mid \bar A_{k-1}) }{ f(A_k \mid \bar A_{k-1}, \bar L_k) },
\]
the weighted (pseudo-)density is proportional to
\[
SW \cdot f(\text{data}) \;\propto\; f(L_0)\; \prod_{k=0}^{K}
\underbrace{f(A_k \mid \bar A_{k-1})}_{\text{depends on past }A\text{ only}} \; f(L_{k+1}\mid \bar A_k, \bar L_k).
\]
Two key consequences:

In the pseudo-population, treatment no longer depends on \(\bar L_k\) at time \(k\) given \(\bar A_{k-1}\). That’s exactly the “as-if randomized given past \(A\)” property we need.
The marginal distribution of treatment given past treatment is preserved (because those \(f(A_k\mid \bar A_{k-1})\) are now the treatment factors in the pseudo-density). This stabilization is what keeps weights moderate and the sample “familiar.”

By contrast, unstabilized weights replace the treatment factor with a constant (intuitively, “flat” assignment), which can make the weighted sample look very unlike the original and push weights to extremes.
A related perspective: unstabilized IPTW is a Horvitz–Thompson–type estimator (unbiased but high variance); stabilized IPTW acts like a Hájek normalization (same target, usually smaller variance, and weights closer to 1).

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: 4 A Napkin-size Numeric Example (one time point)
text:
4 A Napkin-size Numeric Example (one time point)
Suppose 1,000 patients:

800 have low BP (\(L=0\)), 200 have high BP (\(L=1\)).
Doctors treat 20% of low-BP, 80% of high-BP.

So:

\(\Pr(A=1\mid L=0)=0.20\), \(\Pr(A=1\mid L=1)=0.80\).
Overall \(\Pr(A=1)= (160+160)/1000 = 0.32\), \(\Pr(A=0)=0.68\).


Unstabilized Weights

Treated low-BP: weight \(=1/0.20=5\) (big)
Treated high-BP: weight \(=1/0.80=1.25\)
Untreated low-BP: weight \(=1/0.80=1.25\)
Untreated high-BP: weight \(=1/0.20=5\) (big)

Problem: Those 5’s are heavy. Any analysis becomes noisy and sensitive to a few people.


Stabilized Weights

Treated low-BP: \(SW = 0.32/0.20 = 1.60\)
Treated high-BP: \(SW = 0.32/0.80 = 0.40\)
Untreated low-BP: \(SW = 0.68/0.80 = 0.85\)
Untreated high-BP: \(SW = 0.68/0.20 = 3.40\)

Now the largest weight is 3.4, not 5, and most weights are near 1. You still erase the BP→Treatment link in the weighted data, but with less variance.
(You can check: after weighting, the treated fraction in low-BP and high-BP groups both become 0.32—i.e., treatment is independent of BP in the pseudo-population.)

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
One-line Recap
Stabilized weights keep the identification benefits of IPTW but temper extreme weights by reintroducing the right marginal treatment probabilities—so your pseudo-population looks randomized and your estimates are more stable.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Big Idea

Unstabilized IPTW estimates a (counterfactual) mean by adding up outcomes with inverse probabilities and then dividing by N. That’s the Horvitz–Thompson (HT) style: unbiased if the treatment model is correct, but can be high variance when some probabilities are small (huge weights).
Stabilized IPTW (or Hájek style) estimates the same mean by ratio: add up “weighted outcomes” and divide by the sum of weights (not by N). This self-normalizes the weights, yielding smaller variance (typically) with at most tiny finite-sample bias; it’s consistent for the same target.

Think of HT as “plain importance sampling” and Hájek (or stabilized) as “self-normalized importance sampling.”

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Unstabilized IPTW (Horvitz–Thompson)
\[
\widehat{\mu}_{\text{HT}}(1)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\mathbb{I}(A_i=1)\,Y_i}{e(X_i)}.
\]

Unbiased (if \(e(\cdot)\) is correct).
But if some \(e(X_i)\) are small, terms \(1/e(X_i)\) are huge → high variance.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Hájek (ratio) Form
\[
\widehat{\mu}_{\text{H}}(1)=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\mathbb{I}(A_i=1)\,Y_i}{e(X_i)}}
     {\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\mathbb{I}(A_i=1)}{e(X_i)}}.
\]

Same target; weights are self-normalized by \(\sum 1/e\).
Typically smaller variance; slight finite-sample bias that vanishes as \(N\to\infty\).

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
“Stabilized” Weights Viewpoint
Define stabilized weights for treated units as
\[
SW_i=\frac{\Pr(A=1)}{e(X_i)} \quad \text{if } A_i=1,\quad (0 \text{ otherwise}).
\]
Then the ratio estimator with stabilized weights is
\[
\frac{\sum SW_i Y_i}{\sum SW_i}
=\frac{\Pr(A=1)\sum \tfrac{\mathbb{I}(A_i=1)Y_i}{e(X_i)}}
       {\Pr(A=1)\sum \tfrac{\mathbb{I}(A_i=1)}{e(X_i)}}
=\widehat{\mu}_{\text{H}}(1).
\]
So, stabilized IPTW + divide by sum of weights = Hájek.
(Using unstabilized weights but dividing by their sum gives the same ratio.)

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: The Bridge: From Logistic Regression (Log-Odds) to IPW (Probabilities)
text:
The Bridge: From Logistic Regression (Log-Odds) to IPW (Probabilities)
Our goal is to calculate the stabilized weight, which requires the probability of treatment, \(\Prob{A=1 \mid \text{History}}\). But how do we get a number for that probability for each person? We need to model it.
The most common tool for modeling a binary outcome (like treatment vs. no treatment) is logistic regression.

Step 1: The Logistic Model and Its Native Language (Log-Odds)
A logistic regression model does not predict probability directly. Instead, it models the logarithm of the odds (the “logit”) as a linear function of the predictors.
When we fit a model for our treatment \(A\) based on confounders \(L\):
glm(A ~ L1 + L2, family = binomial)
The underlying equation R is solving is:
\(\ln\left(\frac{\Prob{A=1 \mid L}}{1 - \Prob{A=1 \mid L}}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 L_1 + \beta_2 L_2\)
Notice the left side is the log-odds. This is the native language of a logistic model.


Step 2: Translating from Log-Odds to the Probability We Need
For our IPW formula, we don’t want log-odds or odds; we need the clean probability, \(p\). So, we must translate the model’s output back into the language of probability. This is a two-step algebraic conversion:

From Log-Odds to Odds: We exponentiate both sides to undo the natural log (\(\ln\)). \(\text{Odds} = e^{(\beta_0 + \beta_1 L_1 + \beta_2 L_2)}\)
From Odds to Probability: We use the standard conversion formula. \(\text{Probability (p)} = \frac{\text{Odds}}{1 + \text{Odds}}\)

This final probability is exactly what we plug into our weight formula.


Step 3: Putting It Together in R
Fortunately, R’s predict() function handles this translation for us automatically. When you use predict() on a glm object, you can specify the type of output you want.
Let’s use our den_mod_A0_lab model from the lab, which predicted AZT at time 0 based on the baseline CD4 count (L0_cd4).


Code
# We need to run the code from the previous lab to have the model object
set.seed(123)
n_lab <- 500
id <- 1:n_lab
cd4_0 <- rnorm(n_lab, 500, 50)
azt_0_prob <- plogis(-8 + (cd4_0 / 50))
azt_0 <- rbinom(n_lab, 1, azt_0_prob)
hiv_wide_demo <- data.frame(id, L0_cd4 = cd4_0, A0_azt = azt_0)
den_mod_A0_lab <- glm(A0_azt ~ L0_cd4, data = hiv_wide_demo, family = binomial)

# Predict the LOG-ODDS (the model's native output)
log_odds <- predict(den_mod_A0_lab, type = "link")

# Predict the PROBABILITY (what we need for IPW)
probability <- predict(den_mod_A0_lab, type = "response")

# Let's look at the first 5 predictions
data.frame(
  Log_Odds = head(log_odds),
  Probability = head(probability)
)



  



Code
# You can prove they are the same by converting the log-odds manually
manual_probability <- exp(log_odds) / (1 + exp(log_odds))
all.equal(probability, manual_probability)


[1] TRUE


The Workflow in Practice:

You build a logistic model for the denominator (glm(A ~ L, …)).
You build another logistic model for the numerator (glm(A ~ …)).
You use predict(…, type = "response") on both models to get the estimated probabilities for every person.
You plug these predicted probabilities directly into the stabilized weight formula: sw = (p_numerator) / (p_denominator).

So, your intuition about odds was spot-on—they are working under the hood inside the glm function. But for the IPW calculation itself, we use the final translated probability.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: G-Computation vs. MSMs (IPW): A Tale of Two Models
text:
G-Computation vs. MSMs (IPW): A Tale of Two Models
Instead of re-weighting the population, G-computation works by simulating the outcomes for the entire population under different, specific treatment strategies.
The most fundamental difference between these two methods is the model they rely on.








Feature
MSM (via IPW)
G-Computation




Core Idea
Weighting: Create a pseudo-population where confounding is broken.
Simulation: Predict the outcome for everyone under different treatment rules.


Required Model
A model for the treatment assignment: \(\Prob{A \mid L}\)
A model for the outcome: \(\E{Y \mid A, L}\)


Key Strength
Doesn’t require correctly modeling complex interactions in the outcome model.
More stable when you have positivity problems (i.e., near-zero probabilities of treatment).


Key Weakness
Very sensitive to positivity violations (can result in extreme weights).
Very sensitive to getting the outcome model wrong, especially with many confounders.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
The G-Computation Recipe 🍳
G-computation follows a simple and intuitive three-step process to directly estimate the mean potential outcome, \(\E{Y^a}\).

Step 1: Fit a Model for the Outcome
First, we ignore the weights entirely. We fit one, rich regression model that predicts the final outcome using both the treatments and the full confounder history as predictors. This is often called the “Q-model”.
Outcome ~ Treatment_Time_0 + Treatment_Time_1 + Confounder_Time_0 + Confounder_Time_1 …
It’s crucial that this model is specified correctly. Any important interactions between the treatments and confounders must be included.


Step 2: Simulate Potential Outcomes under Intervention
This is the “simulation” or “g-formula” step. We use our model to play God with the dataset.

Copy your dataset twice.
In Copy A, you manually set the treatment variables for every single person to the first strategy. For example, to find the outcome if everyone had been treated at both time points, you would set A0 = 1 and A1 = 1 for all rows.
In Copy B, you set the treatment variables for every single person to the comparison strategy (e.g., A0 = 0 and A1 = 0).
Use the model from Step 1 to predict the outcome for all rows in both of these modified datasets. The predictions from Copy A are the estimated potential outcomes \(\hat{Y}^{\bar{a}=(1,1)}\), and the predictions from Copy B are \(\hat{Y}^{\bar{a}=(0,0)}\).



Step 3: Average and Compare
The final step is straightforward:

Calculate the average of all the predicted outcomes in Copy A. This is your estimate of the mean outcome if everyone had followed the “always treat” strategy, \(\Ehat{Y^{\bar{a}=(1,1)}}\).
Calculate the average of all the predicted outcomes in Copy B. This is your estimate of the mean outcome if everyone had followed the “never treat” strategy, \(\Ehat{Y^{\bar{a}=(0,0)}}\).
The causal effect is the difference between these two averages.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
G-Computation in R
Let’s implement this recipe using our hiv_wide dataset. Our goal is to estimate the effect of the strategy “always take AZT” (A0_azt=1, A1_azt=1) versus “never take AZT” (A0_azt=0, A1_azt=0).

Step 1: Fit the Outcome Model (the “Q-model”)
We regress the final CD4 count on the full treatment and confounder history.


Code
# We are using the hiv_wide data from the previous examples
q_model <- lm(Y_cd4 ~ A0_azt + A1_azt + L0_cd4 + L1_cd4, data = hiv_wide)

summary(q_model)



Call:
lm(formula = Y_cd4 ~ A0_azt + A1_azt + L0_cd4 + L1_cd4, data = hiv_wide)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-63.01 -13.27  -0.55  15.93  62.73 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 107.9458    10.6071   10.18   <2e-16 ***
A0_azt       30.4781     3.3586    9.07   <2e-16 ***
A1_azt       39.1182     2.5901   15.10   <2e-16 ***
L0_cd4       -0.1361     0.0753   -1.81    0.071 .  
L1_cd4        0.8318     0.0913    9.11   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 20.5 on 495 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.806, Adjusted R-squared:  0.805 
F-statistic:  515 on 4 and 495 DF,  p-value: <2e-16




Step 2: Create Intervened-Upon Datasets and Predict
We create two copies and manually set the treatment variables.


Code
# Copy the dataset for the "Always Treat" scenario
d_always_treat <- hiv_wide
d_always_treat$A0_azt <- 1
d_always_treat$A1_azt <- 1

# Copy the dataset for the "Never Treat" scenario
d_never_treat <- hiv_wide
d_never_treat$A0_azt <- 0
d_never_treat$A1_azt <- 0

# Predict potential outcomes for everyone under both scenarios
hiv_wide$y_potential_always <- predict(q_model, newdata = d_always_treat)
hiv_wide$y_potential_never <- predict(q_model, newdata = d_never_treat)

# Look at the results for a few patients
hiv_wide |>
  dplyr::select(id, Y_cd4, y_potential_always, y_potential_never) |>
  head()



  





Step 3: Average and Compare
Now we just take the mean of those two new potential outcome columns.


Code
# Estimate the mean potential outcome under "Always Treat"
mean_y_always <- mean(hiv_wide$y_potential_always)
print(paste("E[Y | Always Treat] =", round(mean_y_always, 2)))


[1] "E[Y | Always Treat] = 499.45"


Code
# Estimate the mean potential outcome under "Never Treat"
mean_y_never <- mean(hiv_wide$y_potential_never)
print(paste("E[Y | Never Treat] =", round(mean_y_never, 2)))


[1] "E[Y | Never Treat] = 429.85"


Code
# Estimate the Average Causal Effect (ACE)
ace_gcomp <- mean_y_always - mean_y_never
print(paste("Average Causal Effect (ACE) =", round(ace_gcomp, 2)))


[1] "Average Causal Effect (ACE) = 69.6"


The estimated average causal effect of this treatment strategy is an increase of 69.6 CD4 points, which is very close to the answer we got with the MSM/IPW approach.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Why variance Shrinks (plain English)

HT’s total weight \(\sum w_i\) can fluctuate wildly sample-to-sample (especially when some \(e(X)\) are tiny), amplifying noise.
Hájek (or stabilized) pins down the total weight (by dividing by \(\sum w_i\)), removing one big source of randomness. That’s the same benefit you get from self-normalized importance sampling.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Many time Points (longitudinal)
At visits \(k=0,\dots,K\):

Unstabilized IPTW (HT-like):

\[
W_i=\prod_{k=0}^K \frac{1}{\Pr(A_{ik}=a_{ik}\mid \bar A_{i,k-1},\bar L_{ik})}.
\]

Stabilized IPTW (Hájek-like):

\[
SW_{i}= \prod_{k=0}^{K} \frac{\Pr(A_{ik} = a_{ik}\mid \bar A_{i,k-1})}{\Pr(A_{ik} = a_{ik}\mid \bar A_{i,k-1},\bar{L}_{ik})}.
\]
You then estimate means or fit an MSM via weighted regression. The numerator factors preserve the marginal treatment process (given past \(A\)) and act like a built-in normalization → weights closer to 1 and smaller variance.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
5 What to Remember in Practice

Same target, better stability. Stabilized weights identify the same MSM parameters but usually with smaller variance.
Mean near 1. With correctly specified models, \(\mathbb{E}(SW)\approx 1\). Analysts often also normalize weights to have mean 1 in the sample (a separate, harmless step).
Numerator model is simple by design. It conditions only on past treatments; do not include covariates affected by prior treatment there.
Still need overlap. If some histories virtually never get a particular treatment (positivity violation), even stabilized weights can be large—consider truncation, coarsening, or redefining the estimand/support.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
6 Two-time Extension (quick peek)
At \(k=0,1\),
\[
SW_i \;=\;
\frac{\Pr(A_{i0}\mid \emptyset)}{\Pr(A_{i0}\mid L_{i0})}
\;\times\;
\frac{\Pr(A_{i1}\mid A_{i0})}{\Pr(A_{i1}\mid A_{i0}, L_{i0}, L_{i1})}.
\]

The first factor stabilizes baseline treatment.
The second factor stabilizes the follow-up decision.

In the weighted world, each decision behaves as if randomized given past treatment, so you can fit a marginal model of the outcome on the treatment history (your MSM) without conditioning on the time-varying confounders that are also mediators.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Motivation and Learning Objectives
In previous lectures, we’ve focused on estimating causal effects when we can measure and adjust for all confounders at a single time point (baseline). But what happens when confounders change over time?
Consider a clinical scenario where doctors adjust a patient’s treatment dose at each visit based on their current health status. That health status is a confounder (it influences the next treatment and the final outcome), but it is also a mediator (it is affected by the previous treatment). This is a time-varying confounder.
If we simply “adjust” for this time-varying confounder in a standard regression model, we will block the causal pathway from the previous treatment to the outcome, which induces bias. This is a classic “collider-stratification” bias. Marginal Structural Models (MSMs) were developed by Robins and colleagues to solve this exact problem.
Learning Objectives: By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

Identify a time-varying confounder affected by prior treatment.
Explain why standard regression and stratification fail in this scenario.
Describe the intuition behind Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW).
Calculate stabilized weights for a simple, two-time-point scenario.
Fit and interpret a basic Marginal Structural Model.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: Why Standard Methods Fail: The Time-Varying Confounder
text:
Why Standard Methods Fail: The Time-Varying Confounder
Let’s visualize the problem with a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
Imagine a two-visit study:

\(A_0\): Treatment at baseline (time 0).
\(L_1\): A health measure at visit 1 (e.g., viral load, blood pressure).
\(A_1\): Treatment at visit 1.
\(Y\): The final health outcome.

The causal structure looks like this:


Code
graph TD
    subgraph Time 0
        A0[A₀: Treatment]
    end

Here, \(L_1\) is our problem variable:

It is a confounder of the \(A_1 \rightarrow Y\) relationship (there is a backdoor path \(A_1 \leftarrow L_1 \rightarrow Y\)).
It is a mediator of the \(A_0 \rightarrow Y\) relationship (it’s on the causal path \(A_0 \rightarrow L_1 \rightarrow Y\)).

If we run a standard regression model like lm(Y ~ A0 + A1 + L1), we are conditioning on \(L_1\). By conditioning on \(L_1\), we adjust for the confounding of the \(A_1 \rightarrow Y\) effect, which is good. However, \(L_1\) is a collider on the path \(A_0 \rightarrow L_1 \leftarrow U_L\) (where \(U_L\) represents unmeasured causes of \(L_1\)). Conditioning on a collider opens a spurious path and biases our estimate of the \(A_0\) effect. More simply, by controlling for \(L_1\), we block the part of \(A_0\)’s effect that goes through \(L_1\), so we no longer estimate the total effect of the treatment plan (\(A_0\) and \(A_1\)).






WarningThe Central Problem



Standard regression models fail with time-varying confounders because conditioning on the confounder (e.g., \(L_1\)) to close a backdoor path simultaneously blocks a causal pathway of interest, biasing the effect estimate for earlier treatments.



💡 The Core Idea: Creating a Pseudo-Population with IPTW
So, if we can’t condition on \(L_1\), what can we do?
The solution is to use Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW) to create a “pseudo-population” in which the treatment is no longer confounded by the measured variables.
The intuition is as follows:

In the real world, a patient’s characteristics (like \(L_1\)) influence the treatment they receive (\(A_1\)). This is confounding.
In an ideal (randomized) world, treatment assignment would be random. It would not depend on \(L_1\).
The MSM approach: We can’t go back in time and randomize, but we can re-weight our observational data to make it look like a randomized trial.

We give a higher weight to individuals who were under-represented in the treatment group they actually received, and a lower weight to those who were over-represented. For example, if sick patients (high \(L_1\)) are much more likely to get treatment \(A_1=1\), we give a large weight to the few healthy patients (low \(L_1\)) who did get \(A_1=1\). This re-weighting creates a balanced pseudo-population where \(L_1\) no longer appears to predict \(A_1\).
Once we have these weights, we can fit a simple marginal model of the outcome on the treatment history, as if we had done a real experiment. This final weighted model is the Marginal Structural Model.

Step 1: Model the Denominator of the Weights
The denominator is the probability of receiving the treatment you actually received, given your past treatment and confounder history.
\[
\pr{A_t=a_t | A_{t-1}=a_{t-1}, L_t=l_t}
\]
We need to estimate this for \(t=0\) and \(t=1\). For simplicity, let’s assume A0 is randomized with \(P(A_0=1)=0.5\).
For A1, we’ll fit a logistic regression model: glm(A1 ~ A0 + L1, family = "binomial").


Code
# Sample Data
dat <- data.frame(
  id = 1:8,
  A0 = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1),
  L1 = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1),
  A1 = c(0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1),
  Y = c(10, 12, 15, 16, 18, 19, 22, 24)
)

# Fit model for the denominator of A1's weight
denom_model_A1 <- glm(
  A1 ~ A0 + L1,
  data = dat,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)
# Get predicted probabilities
dat$pd_A1 <- predict(denom_model_A1, type = "response")

# Probability of receiving the treatment they actually got
dat$p_A1_actual <- ifelse(dat$A1 == 1, dat$pd_A1, 1 - dat$pd_A1)

# Assume A0 was randomized P(A0=1)=0.5
dat$p_A0_actual <- 0.5

print(dat[, c("id", "A0", "L1", "A1", "p_A0_actual", "p_A1_actual")])

The overall denominator for the weight is the product of these probabilities over time: \(d_i = P(A_{i0}) \times P(A_{i1} | A_{i0}, L_{i1})\).


Step 2: Model the Numerator of the Weights (for Stabilization)
The numerator is the probability of receiving the treatment you actually received, given only your baseline confounders. This makes the weights more stable (closer to 1). For our example, we assume no baseline confounders other than \(A_0\). The model is glm(A1 ~ A0, family = "binomial").
\[
P(A_t=a_t | A_{t-1}=a_{t-1})
\]


Code
# Fit model for the numerator of A1's weight
num_model_A1 <- glm(A1 ~ A0, data = dat, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
dat$pn_A1 <- predict(num_model_A1, type = "response")

# Numerator probability
dat$p_num_A1_actual <- ifelse(dat$A1 == 1, dat$pn_A1, 1 - dat$pn_A1)
dat$p_num_A0_actual <- 0.5 # Same as denominator since there are no baseline confounders

print(dat[, c("id", "A0", "A1", "p_num_A0_actual", "p_num_A1_actual")])

The stabilized weight for each person is the cumulative numerator divided by the cumulative denominator.
\[

\]

# Calculate stabilized weight
dat$sw <- (dat$p_num_A0_actual * dat$p_num_A1_actual) /
  (dat$p_A0_actual * dat$p_A1_actual)

Step 4: Fit the Final Marginal Structural Model
Now we fit a weighted linear model to estimate the causal effect of the treatment history (A0, A1) on the outcome Y. Note that we do not include L1 in this final model! The weights have already taken care of its confounding effect.

# Fit the marginal structural model using the weights

msm_fit <- lm(Y ~ A0 + A1, data = dat, weights = sw)

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
🏛️ Key Assumptions and Formalism
For an MSM to yield a valid causal effect, several key assumptions must hold.






TipAssumptions for Marginal Structural Models




Consistency: The observed outcome for an individual with treatment history \(\bar{a}\) is the same as their potential outcome had they received treatment history \(\bar{a}\). \(Y = Y^{\bar{a}}\) if \(\bar{A} = \bar{a}\).
Positivity (or Overlap): For every combination of confounders and past treatment, there is a non-zero probability of receiving any given treatment level. \(P(\bar{A}_t= \bar{a}_t | \bar{L}_t, \bar{A}_{t-1}) > 0\).
No Unmeasured Confounding: We have measured all variables that confound the relationship between treatment and outcome at each time point. This is conditional exchangeability for the entire treatment history: \(Y^{\bar{a}} \indep A_t | \bar{L}_t, \bar{A}_{t-1}\) for all \(t\).




The Formal Model
An MSM for a continuous outcome \(Y\) and treatment history \(\bar{A}=(A_0, A_1, …, A_T)\) is a model for the marginal expectation of the potential outcome, conditional on treatment history:
\[
E[Y^{\bar{a}}] = g(\bar{a}; \psi)
\]
where \(g(\cdot)\) is a function we choose (e.g., linear) and \(\psi\) are the parameters we want to estimate. For our example, the model is:
\[
E[Y^{a_0, a_1}] = \psi_0 + \psi_1 a_0 + \psi_2 a_1
\]
The goal of IPTW is to allow us to fit this model using the observed data.


Concept Check
A researcher is studying the effect of a new blood pressure medication (\(A\)) on risk of heart attack (\(Y\)). Patients are followed for two years. At one year, their blood pressure (\(L_1\)) is measured, and their medication can be adjusted (\(A_1\)). The researcher runs the following model: glm(Y ~ A0 + A1 + L1).
Question: Why is this approach likely to produce a biased estimate of the total causal effect of the treatment strategy (A0 and A1)?
Answer: The variable \(L_1\) (blood pressure at one year) is likely a time-varying confounder affected by prior treatment.

It is affected by the initial treatment \(A_0\) (good medication should lower blood pressure).
It influences the next treatment decision \(A_1\) (doctors might increase the dose if blood pressure is still high).
It influences the final outcome \(Y\) (high blood pressure increases heart attack risk).

By including \(L_1\) in the regression, the researcher is conditioning on a variable that is on the causal pathway from \(A_0\) to \(Y\). This blocks part of \(A_0\)’s effect and can induce collider-stratification bias, leading to an incorrect estimate of the total effect of the treatment plan. An MSM would be a more appropriate method.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
section: How IPTW Formally Breaks the Confounding
text:
How IPTW Formally Breaks the Confounding
Motivation: We’ve claimed that weighting the data with \(sw_i\) creates a pseudo-population where confounding by \(L\) is removed. Let’s see why this is true mathematically for a simple, single-time-point case.
Let \(A\) be a binary treatment, \(L\) a confounder, and \(Y\) an outcome. The standard association is \(E[Y|A=1]\). The causal effect we want is \(E[Y^{a=1}]\). These are not the same if \(L\) confounds the \(A \rightarrow Y\) relationship.
The key assumption is conditional exchangeability: \(Y^a \indep A | L\).
Let’s derive the expectation of the outcome in the weighted population, where the weights are \(w = 1/P(A|L)\).
We want to show that the weighted average of the observed outcome among the treated equals the marginal average of the potential outcome under treatment:
\[
\frac{E[Y \cdot I(A=1) / P(A=1|L)]}{E[I(A=1) / P(A=1|L)]} = E[Y^{a=1}]
\]
where \(I(\cdot)\) is the indicator function.
Let’s work through the numerator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E\left[\frac{I(A=1)Y}{P(A=1|L)}\right] &= E_L\left[E\left[\left.\frac{I(A=1)Y}{P(A=1|L)}\right|L\right]\right] & \text{(By Law of Iterated Expectations)} \\
&= E_L\left[\frac{1}{P(A=1|L)} E[I(A=1)Y | L]\right] & \text{(Treating } P(A=1|L) \text{ as fixed, given } L\text{)} \\
&= E_L\left[\frac{1}{P(A=1|L)} E[Y | A=1, L] P(A=1|L)\right] & \text{(Definition of conditional expectation)} \\
&= E_L[E[Y | A=1, L]] & \text{(The probability terms cancel)} \\
&= E_L[E[Y^{a=1} | A=1, L]] & \text{(By Consistency, } Y = Y^{a=1} \text{ for those with } A=1\text{)} \\
&= E_L[E[Y^{a=1} | L]] & \text{(By Conditional Exchangeability, } Y^{a=1} \indep A|L\text{)} \\
&= E[Y^{a=1}] & \text{(By Law of Iterated Expectations again)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Now the denominator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E\left[\frac{I(A=1)}{P(A=1|L)}\right] &= E_L\left[E\left[\left.\frac{I(A=1)}{P(A=1|L)}\right|L\right]\right] \\
&= E_L\left[\frac{1}{P(A=1|L)} E[I(A=1)|L]\right] \\
&= E_L\left[\frac{1}{P(A=1|L)} P(A=1|L)\right] \\
&= E_L[1] = 1
\end{aligned}
\]
Putting it together, the expectation of the outcome among the treated in the pseudo-population is simply \(E[Y^{a=1}] / 1 = E[Y^{a=1}]\), which is exactly the marginal causal quantity we wanted to estimate. The weighting has successfully removed the confounding influence of \(L\) and allowed us to recover the marginal causal effect from the observed data. This logic extends to the time-varying case with stabilized weights.

title: Inverse Probability Weighting and Marginal Structural Models
text:
Welcome to Week 6. Our journey so far has focused on the point-treatment setting, where we estimate the causal effect of a single exposure assigned at the start of follow-up. We learned to control for baseline confounding using methods like regression, matching, and weighting. However, many of the most critical questions in science, medicine, and public policy involve time-varying treatments, where exposures, confounders, and outcomes are measured repeatedly over time.
This week, we confront one of the most significant challenges in modern observational causal inference: time-varying confounding that is itself affected by past treatment. This dynamic creates a vicious cycle known as treatment-confounder feedback, where a variable today is both a consequence of yesterday’s treatment (a mediator) and a cause of tomorrow’s treatment (a confounder).
We will demonstrate with formal theory and simulations why our standard toolkit—regression adjustment, stratification—fails catastrophically in this scenario. Adjusting for the time-varying confounders using conventional methods can simultaneously block the very causal pathways we wish to study and introduce spurious associations via collider-stratification bias.
The solution to this intricate problem is a powerful and elegant class of methods known as Marginal Structural Models (MSMs). As we will see, MSMs, estimated via a sophisticated application of Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW), allow us to break the feedback loop. By constructing a pseudo-population where confounding is removed at every time point, MSMs enable us to ask and answer causal questions about the effects of entire strategies or histories of treatment, a task that would otherwise be impossible (Hernán & Robins, 2020).

Learning Objectives
By the end of this week’s module and lab, you will be able to:

Define and represent time-varying confounding and treatment-confounder feedback on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), correctly identifying variables that act as both mediators and confounders over time.
Explain with conceptual and graphical arguments why standard regression adjustment fails to estimate the total causal effect of a treatment history in the presence of treatment-confounder feedback.
Define a Marginal Structural Model (MSM) as a model for the marginal mean of a potential outcome under a specified history of treatment, and contrast it with a standard conditional model.
Calculate stabilized inverse probability of treatment weights for longitudinal data by modeling the probability of treatment at each time point, conditional on past treatment and confounder history.
Estimate the parameters of a simple MSM in R by fitting a weighted regression model to a pseudo-population and correctly interpreting the resulting coefficients as the causal effects of a treatment strategy.
